speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 30, 1988, the Government tabled Bill C-139, an Act to amend the Income Tax Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal-Post Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, 1977, and certain related Acts, a brick of some 500 pages.
I find that not only is it complex and difficult but, to make matters worse, the Government did not append an index to this Bill. For those of us who are not specialists in this field, it is next to impossible to read the Bill. I know that members of the Government sometimes read Bills, and that sometimes Ministers use Bills to inform us as to what is in them. However, I wonder if you, Mr. Speaker, having read this Bill, found it easy to read such a Bill without an index.
In days gone by, members of the Conservative Party would have given hell to the Liberals if we so much as came in with a Bill that did not have an index in it, a Bill one third the size of this Bill. As a matter of fact, the Government has the habit of putting in an index. That is what it did with respect to Bill

subtopic: REQUEST FOR IN DEX TO B1LL C-139

I do not remember any income tax legislation as progressive from the previous Liberal administration. Second, I do not remember any indexes.
I will make inquiries to see if it is possible to prepare an index, if one is not already in existence, and report back to my hon. friend and the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REQUEST FOR IN DEX TO B1LL C-139

I am pleased that the Hon. Minister of State has indicated that perhaps he can find some way to accommodate the Hon. Member, although I believe the Government is probably within the rules procedurally.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to present a petition which is signed by citizens of Saint John, New Brunswick, and a number of adjoining towns and townships. The petition has been certified correct as to form
and content. It indicates that when the issue of such fundamental importance to the future of Canada as the proposed trade pact with the United States of America comes before Parliament, it is the opinion of the petitioners that the people of Canada should be permitted an opportunity to vote to accept or reject such a trade pact before it is put into force.

subtopic: PETITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two petitions to present today. The first petition deals with the trade deal between Canada and the United States. It points out that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had no mandate to negotiate this deal, that it would reduce Canada's ability to plan economic, social, and cultural programs, and that it would integrate Canada further into the North American defence industrial base.
Therefore, the petitioners call for a national debate on the trade deal, and that this debate result in a national general election before the agreement comes into effect.

subtopic: PETITIONS
subsubtopic: LOW-LEVEL FLIGHTS OVER GOOSE BAY, LABRADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the second petition deals with low-level flight training of pilots of NATO at the Canadian Forces Base at Goose Bay, Labrador. The petition points out that it disrupts the way of life of the native people, that hunting, fishing, tourism, and mining can provide more stable, healthy, and peaceful employment than this type of training, and that this training is provocative in terms of flying under radar in eastern Europe, and therefore endangers world peace.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to ensure that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) ends all low-level flight training at the Goose Bay Canadian Forces Base.

The petitioners state that the Conservative Government had no mandate from the Canadian people to conclude a free trade agreement with the United States. The petitioners state that the proposed trade agreement would deny Canada policy freedom to determine its own economic future, and undermine our ability to build a society distinct from that of the United States.
Therefore, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to dissolve and allow the people of Canada the opportunity to accept or reject the proposed free trade agreement during a national general election.

Mr. Speaker, in case there had been some request for debate, I prepared a few remarks that I would like to put on the record now.
I think it is fair to say that the subject of free trade has been in the public domain for some time. The issue has been studied by two parliamentary committees which held extensive hearings and travelled across Canada. I do not think in my meagre experience in this House there has been any issue that has so consistently dominated the period for Standing Order 21, the Question Period, Opposition Days, and speeches on various Bills. The issue of free trade has very definitely been in the public and in the parliamentary forum. I would say that this time allocation debate and motion is not about five days debate on Bill C-130, it is about the conclusion of the debate on the issue of free trade.
We on the government side, Madam Speaker, feel it is time to decide. I would point out that the by the time we are finished debating this Bill we will have had four long days- excessively long days because we are in a period of extended hours-and one short day. When we originally discussed this matter with counterparts opposite, the Opposition House Leaders, we offered three long days and two short days under the usual formula of time. We did that with a view to receiving a counter-offer. At no time did we receive a counter-offer which we could then mull over and come back to the House Leaders, our caucus and Cabinet with. No counter offer was made.

I see the ex-Leader of the NDP in the provincial legislature here today. I would hope that he would see fit to enter into the debate today and to participate during the time allocated.
Because my time is limited to 10 minutes and I may not have an opportunity to participate in the debate, I want to say something about the issue of free trade, if I may. There are two points that I want to make, and they are connected to why we have to decide this now. Our opponents are wrapping themselves in the flag and declaring that we have sold out our sovereignty. That is nonsense. Years after the creation of the European Common Market, there is still a Spain, a United Kingdom, a Germany and an Italy.
Those opposite call themselves nationalists and say that they are the only true Canadians. The Canadians who are going to build a stronger Canada, the Canadians who have some faith in the future, are the Canadians who are in favour of this Bill. We do not have to take a back seat to anyone when it comes to sovereignty because our record is full of initiatives which establish our sovereignty as a country.
I am talking about the multiculturalism Bill which is at report stage, I am talking about the Official Languages Act, Bill C-72. We announced a water policy. We have an Environmental Protection Act which was passed and given Royal Assent. The Atlantic Opportunities Agency, the Western Diversification Fund, the National Defence White Paper and the construction of an Arctic-class ice-breaker are on the record.
This Government awarded for the first time the contract to monitor our North Warning System to a Canadian firm. We took it away from the Americans who had it for 30 years under previous Liberal administrations. That is sovereignty. Sovereignty means being able to look after yourself. It means believing it and demonstrating it. Strong countries execute international agreements with other countries. Weak countries are afraid.

That brings me to the comments of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who said that this agreement is a declaration of confidence in ourselves, of confidence in our ability to compete with the best in the world, of confidence in our ability to adapt in a tough and demanding international environment.

There is small Canada right over there. Big Canada says we can compete with the Americans and small Canada has a massive inferiority complex. Big Canada says we can coexist with our neighbours and small Canada wraps itself in the flag and says it is afraid. Big Canada looks to the free trade agreement as a basis for prosperity and little Canada has no alternative.
This is an agreement for the 21st century. It has disappeared. It has been replaced by the Republican Party of the North.
We now have in Canada a Government that is headed by someone who ran a branch plant. He now has a branch plant Party. He wants to turn Canada into a branch plant country. The Progressive Conservative Party, the Party of John A. Macdonald, the Party that used to stand for Canadians' opportunity to make choices of their own, that used to use the instruments of Government as an effective way to build a nation, has now disappeared into the branch plant Republican Party of North America.

I am here partly to lament the passing of that institution, because it did represent something that was important. I disagreed with its policies, but at least it had Canadians roots and Canadian outlooks and it respected Parliament.
Now that that institution has disappeared and we have this Republican Party of the North appearing in the House, we have to recognize that the only way to deal with it is simply to say that it is an alien force with a series of alien ideas and a very alien attitude. The real victim is the place in which we stand today, our own Parliament. The Republican Party of the North does not recognize the value of a parliamentary system. It does not recognize the opportunity that Canadians must have for a proper debate.
The Minister of State (Mr. Lewis), the Government House Leader, has tried to perpetuate the myth that there have been all kinds of opportunity for debate. Let us look at the record. A committee in the summer of 1985 looked at two issues, the star wars issue and the concept of free trade. The recommendations it brought to the House were all rejected by the Government. Not one was adopted. The primary recommendation was that there should be a parliamentary debate in the House of Commons to establish a mandate for the Government to negotiate a trade deal in order to ensure that before the negotiations even began, there would be the opportunity for Canadians to know what they were getting into. That recommendation was rejected by the Government.
The first committee was thrown in the ashcan in typical fashion. The second committee to which the Government House Leader referred was established just before Christmas before it had the final agreement. It did not even have the details of the agreement. It did not know what kind of arrangements were going to be made.
We have to recognize that there is a major difference between the concept and the application. A real estate agent might say to me: "I would like to sell you a house," and I would say "I would like to buy a house". However, before I buy it, I look at the contract. I see what interest rates I am paying. I see what the terms of payment will be. I see what the obligations of the buyer and the seller will be. However, this Government does not want us to look at the contract. It does not want us to see what the specific obligations, rights and duties will be.
The Government is saying that this is just a debate about the concept of free trade, a debate about the concept of motherhood, fatherhood or sisterhood. The fact is that we have to see what the deal is. No Parliament has yet had the opportunity to look specifically at the deal that is now on the table.
The Government is giving us a couple of days to have a few rounds at it. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), Canada's answer to illiteracy, is now saying that he will not even allow the committee itself to cross the country to

ensure that Canadians from New Brunswick to British Columbia, Canadians who will be directly affected, will have the opportunity to be heard.

Already we have the threat of the Government using its majority to simply ride roughshod over the right of Canadians to have their case heard and representations made on their behalf.

We can cite Bill after Bill where this Parliament has had a fair opportunity to be heard. Yet an omnibus Bill which will affect 28 Acts of Parliament covering energy, investment, agriculture, natural resources, indeed every part of Canada, will not be debated because there is insufficient time for Members to make their case. That is an incredible example of the kind of arrogance and indifference the Government shows toward the parliamentary process.
There is no way it can be sugar coated. There is no way the Government can create the big lie that there has been a full opportunity to be heard. I defy any member of the Conservative Party to stand up and tell us how much time we have spent in debate on the hundreds of pages of the Bill now before this House. I will tell them. I think members of the Conservative Party should be well aware of the latest poll published on Friday which shows that since they announced this initiative two and a half years ago, when they had 70 per cent in support, their support has dropped to a minority. Madam Speaker, to understand fully the meaning of our debate, I think it would be worth taking at least a few minutes to see exactly what is involved, and it cannot be pointed out too often that Canada is an exporting country. In referring to this debate and the Free Trade Agreement, this basic fact must be borne in mind. Canada is probably the country whose gross domestic product depends most on its exports. That means Canada is probably the country that depends most on its exports to put bread and butter on the table. That, in essence, is Canada. And everyone agrees that this is so; even my colleagues in the federal Liberal Party and my colleague in the New Democratic Party agree. The fact is that more than one of every three jobs in Canada depends on exports.
Plainly the issue we are debating today is by no means an insignificant one for us, for our country. That is clear. If more than one Canadian in three depends on exports for their jobs, then this question is of the utmost importance. It is a question of the utmost importance when you look at our relations with the United States, because 80 per cent of our exports go to the United States. Around 23 per cent of our gross domestic product here in Canada depends on our trade with the United States. That is what we are talking about today. So it is a question of the utmost importance.
Madam Speaker, the three federal political Parties agree on the fact that Canada is an exporting country, and that it must remain an exporting country. The divergence of opinion comes when we discuss the means that must be employed to try to maintain our existing export capacity.

In recent years there has been an important change of perspective, I think, a change that must be taken into account and that must be explained more clearly, so that the people of Canada can understand their government's motivation. I am referring here to our attitude, if you like, our political will, our approach to trade, from the Second World War to roughly the 1980s. During that period, that is to say since World War II, there has been an intensification of the economies of Canada and the United States, which was accelerated by the war effort.
From that time to the 1980s, Canada's perspective on its trade relations was always more or less the same. Our intention, our will, were always directed toward being able to diversify our trade relations, because we realized that we were very dependent on a single market, that of the United States. To give you an idea of the form this took, in 1960 Prime Minister Diefenbaker wanted to diversify our trade relations toward Great Britain, arguing that we should not put all our eggs in one basket. That was the political thinking of the day. In 1976, the Trudeau government signed a general agreement with the European Economic Community, with about the same aim in view as Mr. Diefenbaker had had: to diversify our trade relations toward partners other than the United States, because we were largely dependent, and at the time thought to be too dependent, on that one market.
In 1980 the so-called third option was formulated, that is to say, an attempt to step up trade relations, this time with the developing countries, with, as always, the additional objective of making ourselves less dependent on the American market.
Madam Speaker, the great change occurred in the early years of this decade, particularly after the recession. The approach changed, and instead of having a continental vision of its trade, Canada has slowly but surely developed a more global vision of its policy and international trade.
The first sign of change occurred in 1982, when a Senate Committee, mandated in 1974 to study our relations with the United States, published a report which I can only assume my Liberal colleagues know well, since it was they who published it in 1982. This report recommended that the government of the day sign a free trade agreement with the United States.
So this is not a new proposal. And when my colleague from Winnipeg tells us that he has not studied the report, and that this is a question that has simply appeared from nowhere, and that we are going into it with our eyes closed-well, then I think there is quite a gap between that and the facts, Madam Speaker. Already in 1982 there was a Senate Committee, chaired by a Liberal Senator, recommending unanimously that we sign a free trade agreement with the United States.
And what did the Liberal government of the day do? In 1983 it issued a discussion paper on that very topic, Canada's trade relations. Again in 1983, in one of its Speeches from the Throne, the Liberal government of the day announced its intention of undertaking sectoral negatiations, Madam

The two Ministers, American and Canadian, submitted their reports to their respective Heads of Government, the Prime Minister and the President, recommending that they undertake negotiations with a view to signing a free trade agreement. But the final touch was undoubtedly the publication of the Macdonald Commission report, on September 5, 1985. This Commission was chaired by a former Liberal Finance Minister, Donald Macdonald, who recommended unequivocally that the Canadian government undertake negotiations to reach an agreement on free trade with the United States.
I will point out in passing that Mr. Macdonald, your former Liberal Minister of Finance, today supports the free trade agreement that we are recommending to the country.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I oppose this motion and I must begin by saying that it is shocking to see a Minister of the Crown treating a question of such great importance to our country with such lightness and frivolity.
We have in front of us the most important issue on which any Parliament in our entire history has had to make a decision. And all we get from these Ministers are weak jokes, instead of a debate on the substance of the question before us. And that question is: should we limit to only one more day debate on second reading of Bill C-130?
Madam Speaker, the Minister who just spoke, and the Acting Parliamentary House Leader, spoke of question periods, they spoke of committee studies, they spoke of discussions with the public, but there is a large hole in their argument because none of this public consultation, none of these Royal Commissions, none of these Senate Committees, none of these Committees, none of these discussions, dealt with bill C-130 or, more importantly still, with the Mulroney-
Time Allocation
Reagan Free Trade Agreement which the Bill attempts to bring into effect.

The Deputy Government House Leader and the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) have given us a long catalogue of events at which time they allege there was discussion of the free trade deal with the United States, entered into by the Conservative Government.
I suggest that there is a fundamental flaw in that argument. None of those committee hearings, none of those royal commissions, none of those exchanges in Question Period dealt in any way, shape or form, in a parliamentary sense, with the deal signed by the Conservative Government and the Government of Ronald Reagan. Specifically, they did not deal in any formal, parliamentary way with Bill C-130. It is a Bill designed to change 28 Acts of Parliament in order to make that trade deal with the United States come into effect.
What the Government is saying is that not only does it have no respect for the sovereignty and independence of the country, but at the same time it shows this by saying that it has no respect for the fundamental means of operation of our parliamentary institutions. If it had respect for the parliamentary institutions of the country, and therefore for the sovereignty and independence of the country, it would not try to choke off debate on the most important question to come before this House since Confederation after only four or five days of debate.
What does the Government have to fear by allowing the same type of discussion to carry on that the Conservative Party, when it was in opposition, insisted on and received from other Governments on measures far less important, far less serious than the trade deal with the United States? I remember the months and months and months that the Conservative Party took on measures such as the National Transportation Act and the Crow rate, both very important measures, but certainly not as fundamental as this trade deal with the United States. It would not accept this type of limitation. Yet measures of the type I have mentioned, as important as they are and as important as they were, were not as broad-ranging and as fundamental as the Government's trade deal with the United States.
I give you, Madam Speaker, one example of the absolute folly, the foolishness of the Government in trying to choke off debate on second reading of its trade deal with the United States. As yet there has not been presented to the Congress of the United States the American legislation to implement its side of the trade deal. We do not know yet exactly what it will be. We have seen the drafting instructions. But these drafting instructions are subject to negotiation between the Congress and the President. This legislation was promised to the Congress weeks ago but we have not seen it yet. We do not know exactly when it will come forward. We do not know to

July 4, 1988
Time Allocation
what extent it will tilt the Government's trade deal with the United States even further in the direction of the United States than the deal does already.
Surely it is the height of folly, a lack of real concern for the well-being of this country to try to proceed with the Bill to implement the trade deal with the United States before we know what this American legislation will state, and before we know how the Congress will react to it. This is exactly the same type of irresponsibility we have seen connected with the Government's approach to its trading relations with the United States from the very moment it came into office.
What we now have from the other side is nothing but a pile of stale jokes. First, just in the last few days we had the Minister who is in charge of this measure saying that he had not even bothered to read the deal all the way through and yet he expected Canadians to accept his salesmanship of this deal. He said that he used to sell vacuum cleaners but he never vacuumed a house. How shameful it is for the Minister for International Trade to deal with the future of the country in the same way he used to deal with vacuum cleaners. This country is more important, no matter what the Conservatives think, than a vacuum cleaner. However, when the next election comes the Conservative Party will be vacuumed up and right out of office.
If the Government really did not fear the reaction of the Canadian public to its legislation, if it really had a vision of a big Canada as distinct from a vision of a small Canada, it would say: "We don't mind that this debate goes on for several more weeks. We will also say that when this debate comes to a natural end we will allow full committee hearings across the country". In so saying this Government would say that it has confidence in itself, in its ideas, including this trade deal that it negotiated with the United States.
By trying to choke off debate at this point the Government is saying to the Canadian people that it lacks confidence in itself and in its ideas. It is saying that it knows the more the idea of the trade deal is studied and discussed and then understood by the Canadian people, the less the Canadian people will like it. This Government is showing its lack of confidence in itself. It is showing its lack of confidence in Canada. When it says, as the Minister says, that it stands for a big Canada, the vision of the Government of a big Canada is one absorbed into the United States so that there will be one big North American country dominated by Washington.
What happened to the vision of Sir John A. Macdonald which was brought forward so gloriously on July 1, 1867? What happened to the vision of successive Conservative Prime Ministers? Mr. Diefenbaker would not have gone for this deal. He would have stood up and said exactly what he thought of the cowardly and fearful Government that has replaced his vision. The current Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) did not do this. He would not have done this.
If we want to look at a non-parliamentary expression of this deal, if that counts as much as discussion and formal decision
in Parliament does, then why does the Conservative Party not look at the words of its Leader when he was seeking to head the Party? He said that when it comes to free trade with the United States, it would undermine our sovereignty and he would have none of it now or at any other time. If nonparliamentary discussion counts for the Conservative Party, then let it give full weight to the words of its current Leader when he sought the leadership of his Party and when he seemed to be speaking for all time. We now see how empty those words were, just like everything else he has been saying ever since, just like everything the Conservative Party has been saying.
The Conservative Party does not care about Parliament. In presenting this motion it showed that it does not care about Canada. That is why we should vote against this motion and press the Government to call an election as soon as possible so that it can be shown that while the Conservative Party does not care about Canada, Canadians care about their country. They will get rid of the Government. They will be the ones who will save Canada.

From the beginning it was made clear what would not be at issue in the negotiations-our political sovereignty, our unique cultural identity, our social programs, or our commitment to fight regional disparities.
When the federal Government embarked on negotiating freer trade with the U.S. we understood that Canada, and all its regions, depend on trade for our prosperity. We set out to achieve a bilateral agreement with the United States, our largest trading partner, while at the same time pursuing global negotiations and initiatives.
In my view the freer trade agreement negotiated with the United States presents eastern Ontario with its greatest opportunity ever to catch up with other parts of this, our great Province of Ontario, and other manufacturing sectors. Furthermore, it allows us to maintain a share in high quality, high-skilled jobs which young people seek as their future career choices, their future career options.

I mentioned earlier that I favoured time allocation because we must move with this important trade legislation to get on with the governing of the country, not the frivolousness the NDP and its social policies. To date, opponents of free trade have fought this initiative not through engaging the federal Government in debate on the merits of what the agreement contains, but by raising the spectre of dangers that do not exist, a process designed to confuse the public.
Thomas d'Aquino, President of the Business Council on National Issues, has characterized those tactics as "intellectual terrorism". The opposition Parties would have the public believe that free trade is a threat to our culture, our social programs, our identity as a distinct people, and will inevitably lead to the loss of thousands of jobs.
This is not the first time that the federal Government has heard such criticism from the opposition Parties. One point that should be stressed is the opponents of free trade are largely those who said that our other policies would doom the nation; that the pursuit of deficit reduction was single-minded cruelty which would cost the country thousands of jobs. We endured that criticism then, and we persevered in our policies because we knew we were right. They said our policies would cost tens of thousands of jobs. We said our policies would create an environment in which tens of thousands of jobs would be created.
Time Allocation
Over 1,228,000 jobs have been created since 1984. In my riding of Hastings-Frontenac-Lennox and Addington, unemployment is now at its lowest point in over a decade. With such new industries as Goodyear and D. & E. Wood and the multiplier effect that this will have, unemployment will be reduced and new economic activities will be created.
These are the national results of national policies. These are the job creating industries and are not only producing for Canadian markets, but for North American and world markets. The results will be a boon to eastern Ontario, and an opportunity for youth and for jobs in this country.
When people attempt to hold up government legislation as important as Bill C-130,1 have no alternative but to support a Government that wants to get on with governing and doing what is right for the people of Canada who want to work.
Under the free trade agreement, for the first time, world-class Ontario businessmen and services will be able to expand and grow as they seize the new opportunities available through this agreement. The new rules governing services and regarding temporary work in the United States will put our service industries and professionals on a level playing field. There is no part of Canada better positioned to seize these opportunities than the border regions of eastern Ontario.
A second sector for opportunity in this area is our manufacturing sector. This agreement will enable the manufacturing sector to grow from its Canadian base, encouraging new investment in world-scale Canadian enterprises. No province has more to gain under free trade than Ontario. Its economy was built on trade with the United States. Today, 90 per cent of Ontario's exports go to the United States. In turn, the United States provides 83 per cent of Ontario's imports.
In addition to the benefits offered by free trade's phase-out of tariffs over 10 years, we stand to gain from the $4 billion U.S. government purchasing market which will now be opened to Ontario firms. This is of particular importance to eastern Ontario. We have sought this opportunity for more than 20 years, and firms, particularly in my riding, are ready and able to take advantage of it.
It should be no surprise then that spokesmen for our manufacturing sector have called this agreement a great agreement for Canada and welcome it with open arms. When I hear the enthusiasm of existing industries and their plans for expansion through a freer trade agreement, I am convinced that the days of eastern Ontario being short-changed in manufacturing and employment opportunities are numbered.
Another opportunity lies in resource industries, both agriculture and forestry. I recognize that some people were worried about free trade posing a threat to the dairy industry. It is not surprising that they were frightened. The critics of free trade were consciously raising that fear. Of course, they were the same people who said our economic program would cause a loss of thousands of jobs. They were wrong about the jobs, and they were wrong about marketing boards. As

Dairy farmers will continue to enjoy the income stability of long term federal dairy policy which the Government has implemented.
In the forestry sector, industry should benefit from the gradual reduction of tariffs, barriers which have prevented us from processing wood even further prior to export-exporting jobs. That is extremely important for the region, because value added processing creates the potential for more jobs to be created here in Ontario.
Finally, a very important factor in the future development of eastern Ontario is small business development. The federal Government has introduced a variety of policies since 1984 to encourage small business development in Canada. We believe that the free trade agreement will further stimulate this growth. That is not only our opinion. It is the opinion of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business. Federation President John Bullock has stated that small business in this country should be excited about the opportunities for greater investment in Canada, terming the agreement a "once in a lifetime opportunity for Canada" which will also help us with greater European and Asian investment.
More important, secure access to the United States market means that future Canadian business growth can take place here in Canada. It means we should at least see an end to the exodus of eastern Ontario firms when wanting to expand, set up shop across the border as a means of getting around U.S. trade barriers. The free trade agreement secures the gains already made, and opens new windows of opportunity for greater growth.
I have outlined why I believe free trade is eastern Ontario's best bet for greater diversification and more growth, and why I support time allocation. I do so because I believe the greatest danger to our Canadian way of life lies not in the prosperity of freer trade, but lies in the property of protectionism, and our inability to afford regional development and social and cultural programs which reflect Canadian values.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DOWNING OF IRANIAN AIRLINER BY UNITED STATES NAVAL VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the destruction of 290 lives aboard an Iranian passenger plane as it crossed the Persian Gulf yesterday is an action that cries out to heaven. For its cruel and final nature, it ranks with the shooting down of the Korean airliner in 1983 when innocent lives were also taken for the same argument, namely, that the off-course airplane allegedly posed a threat.
There is a peculiar similarity between the two superpowers in reacting to the two tragic events. Both expressed regret about the shooting, but still defended the legitimacy of such an act. Where the similarity ends is with the unwarranted presence in the Persian Gulf of the U.S. fleet engaged in a role that endangers more the seeking of peace in that region than it prevents war.
As a parliamentarian, I wish to put on record my sense of grief and horror at this senseless act in the hope that you, Mr. Speaker, will transmit it to Iranian and American parliamentarians. Our sorrow is about the fact that such a tragedy can still happen, that innocent civilians die because of unjustifiable and condoned acts of war-mongering.

July 4, 1988

subtopic: TREATMENT OF WEALTHY PROSPECTIVE IMMIGRANTS
TREATMENT OF WEALTHY PROSPECTIVE IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on behalf of the thousands of Canadians, many of whom live in my city of Winnipeg, who are seeking to reunify their families through the legal procedures set down in our Immigration Act. They follow the law despite knowing that reunification will face long delays because Immigration Canada is woefully understaffed, particularly in Asiatic countries.
If a would-be immigrant is a wealthy business person, the story is quite different. There are immigration consultants and lawyers in Canada who are busily soliciting clients in places
like Hong Kong, offering Canadian citizenship for those wealthy enough to qualify for the business classification. Yet these same business people are told by their advisers that Canadian law is so full of loopholes that it is not necessary to give up present citizenship, to set up legitimate investments in Canada, or even to live in Canada at all.
Is this the kind of law we want for persons entering Canada? Is this the kind of person we want entering Canada? Is this fair treatment for the thousands of Canadians who are following the law to get family members into Canada? The answer to these questions is an emphatic no, and the Government must implement a fairer system for all future Canadians.

subtopic: WESTERN DROUGHT-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
WESTERN DROUGHT-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pride, as a Conservative, that I rise today to bring to the attention of the House that the Government is to provide up to $76.5 million to help western livestock producers cope with the drought that is devastating the Prairies. Together with the provincial Governments, this initiative will assist producers with up to $153 million. This will include a payment for breeding livestock in severely hit areas of up to $60 per head.
The Saskatchewan producers will receive up to $39 million under this plan. For Alberta and Manitoba, the figures are $44 million and $17 million.
The drought relief package will also provide payment of $15 an acre for greenfeed assistance, up to a total of $53 million. This is a boost to the supply of feed and a help for soil conservation.
Together the programs address the drought situation in a comprehensive way and the per head payment allows producers themselves to act in a way that best suits their individual operations. The Government has once again illustrated its strong commitment to the needs of Canadian agriculture and will continue to do so in the future.

maintopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON BIRTH TECHNOLOGY
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON BIRTH TECHNOLOGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for months now, researchers in the fields of medicine, ethics, and the law have been calling on the Government to set up a Royal Commission to explore the emerging field of birth technology.
July 4, 1988

I personally have called upon the Government to react to these calls in this very House.
I rise again today because, tragically, we have reached a point where our scientific knowledge exceeds our abilities to make decisions in this field, and some form of action must be taken. This is a moral, social and political issue that cannot be ignored. To do so would be to condemn our society to live with the consequences of the unregulated contracting out of wombs, the possibility of unregulated fetal experimentation, and the commercialization of our most basic relationships. Once again I call on the Government to set up a Royal Commission in the hope that it will address its responsibilities.

subtopic: DROUGHT ASSISTANCE PACKAGE WELCOMED
DROUGHT ASSISTANCE PACKAGE WELCOMED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to commend the Government for proving again that it supports Canadian farmers. As is the habit of this Government, it has consulted broadly with provincial officials and the producers before announcing its part of the $ 153-million drought aid package. This package is designed to help all livestock producers and allows them to choose from an array of options.
Producers can decide if they wish to transport cattle to feed or feed to cattle. They can choose to sell their cattle and restock next year without a tax penalty. Late seeding to produce greenfeed is encouraged.
Grain farmers in western Canada and Ontario still face the damage brought on by this drought. Last week the drought damage in my riding was severely compounded by frost. I know that grain farmers can expect a reasoned response from the Government.
As a member of the Ontario caucus, I applaud the actions of the Government and its support of western farmers. This Government has shown farmers again that when it states its commitment to farmers it can be believed without question.

subtopic: POLL FAVOURING IMPROVED SERVICE OVER PROFITS
POLL FAVOURING IMPROVED SERVICE OVER PROFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Saturday's Montreal Gazette reported on a public opinion poll which indicated that 70 per cent of Canadians want Canada Post to put improved service before profits. It went on to
indicate that the survey, conducted by Angus Reid Associates, found that the vast majority would prefer to receive the best possible postal service, even if it means a post office budget deficit that would have to be covered by tax dollars.
There has been a battle of the polls with the Government. This is a scientific poll done on a random sample basis. The kind of polls the Government has been quoting have been done in selected communities and are not random samples. As well, the questions have been biased. It is time for the Government to recognize that Canadians want good postal service. Canadians want the Government to watch the pennies, but they want it to provide service as the number one priority.
To be fair, the poll also indicated that 22 per cent said that the Crown corporation's top priority should be to avoid losing money. That is the portion of the population that the Government is playing to, the portion of the population that will support the cuts in rural services and discriminatory policies in suburban locations.
It is time for the Government to get its priorities straight, to hear what the Opposition is saying and to understand that the Opposition is reflecting public opinion. It is time the Government stopped accusing us of lying when we represent the majority in Canada and we ask for service to be the number one priority at the Post Office rather than the under-cutting of the service Canadians receive.

subtopic: SENATE'S DELAY IN PASSING AMENDING LEGISLATION
SENATE'S DELAY IN PASSING AMENDING LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as each day passes, the backlog in Canada's refugee processing system grows larger. The backlog could reach 80,000 by the end of the year, and if an election were to be held now, government Bills C-55 and C-84 presently in the Senate would die. The backlog would double before new legislation could be drawn up and passed.
The Liberal controlled other place is responsible for making Canada a haven for bogus refugees, as well as harming our integrity and reputation in the world community. The Canadian taxpayer is footing the full bill for these individuals, of whom the overwhelming majority are liars and cheaters.
What a shame that the Liberal controlled other place, after a year of studying the two Bills, is placing cheap partisan politics above the interests of Canada and Canadians.

July 4, 1988

subtopic: REQUEST THAT 10-WEEK ELIGIBILITY PERIOD FOR BENEFITS BE RETAINED
REQUEST THAT 10-WEEK ELIGIBILITY PERIOD FOR BENEFITS BE RETAINED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of South East New Brunswick still have no news about the eligible period for unemployment insurance. Since May 10, when the Department of Employment and Immigration extended the eligible period from ten to sixteen weeks, residents of South East New Brunswick have been signing endless petitions to object to this decision. Workers in South East New Brunswick want the Minister to know how hard it is to find employment for more than ten weeks. Those who work in fish processing plants cannot work for more than ten weeks because in some cases the fishing season only lasts that long.
The New Brunswick Minister of Labour, the Hon. Mike McKee, has met the Minister in order to discuss this problem and find a solution. The Minister of Employment and Immigration must realize that she will make things very difficult for workers in New Brunswick if she still decides to change the eligible period. I suggest the Minister should find a way to apply separate standards for urban and rural areas. The unemployment rate in rural areas is three times as high as in urban centres.

subtopic: WESTERN DROUGHT-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
WESTERN DROUGHT-FEDERAL ASSISTANCE FOR LIVESTOCK PRODUCERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday, June 30, a program relating to livestock producers affected by the drought was announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise). To help producers maintain breeding herds the program will provide $100 million in per head payments for breeding stock in designated drought areas, as well as $53 million in payments on a $15 per acre basis for greenfeed and late seeded crops.
While the funding will be helpful, a most important aspect of the program was the announcement of tax deferral for producers who have to deplete their breeding herds as a result of these drought conditions. For many years the Canadian Cattlemen's Association requested a program of tax deferral in circumstances such as we now face. When forced sales of breeding stock take place the tax triggered makes it difficult if not impossible to rebuild the herds when conditions improve.
This is a common sense, practical approach in the best longterm interests of the industry. It does not cost taxpayers money. It does not avoid taxes. Most important, it gives the
individual livestock producer an opportunity to make the right management decision in his particular circumstances.
These changes are long overdue and I commend the Government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) for responding to a legitimate concern of the industry with a simple, straightforward and practical solution.

subtopic: DOWNING OF IRANIAN AIRLINER BY UNITED STATES NAVAL VESSEL
DOWNING OF IRANIAN AIRLINER BY UNITED STATES NAVAL VESSEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the NDP I wish to express shock and disapproval at the downing of an Iranian civilian airliner by an American warship in the Persian Gulf yesterday. I wish to express profound regret at the tragic loss of over 290 lives.
While the full facts behind this incident have yet to be revealed, we urge the Canadian Government to join in calling for an emergency meeting of the UN Security Council and for a full UN sponsored inquiry. Both sides must co-operate in the full disclosure of messages, perceptions, and decisions made in the crisis moments leading up to the shooting. Canada must clearly communicate its disapproval to the Iranians over any acts of retribution.
This indefensible incident raises the question of U.S. deployment of air and naval forces in the Persian Gulf. Rather than discouraging attacks on shipping, they have led to increased instability and greater mutual threat. With the destructive power deployed and the tensions rampant in this region, such incidents are likely to recur.
A common security framework for the Persian Gulf must be pursued, rather than mutually antagonistic military postures. UN Resolution 598 calling for a ceasefire in the Gulf war must be reinforced with strong and comprehensive sanctions, including an arms embargo.

subtopic: CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
CRITICISM OF GOVERNMENT POLICIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, deregulation, privatization, and Americanization are the package which the Government has developed as a vehicle for putting Canada under the economic control of American multinationals. All three moves are based on an ideology which accepts the tenet that large corporations have the right to direct the economy of the country, indeed of the world.
Which of these policies is going to help the ordinary Canadian achieve a better life? Who do these policies benefit? Deregulation allows multinationals to operate with fewer controls. Privatization allows the Government to pass over to its multinational friends the fruits of the taxpayers' development of many years. Americanization is the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal which turns over Canadian resources to prop up the faltering economy of the U.S.
Deregulation, privatization, and Americanization, the three horsemen of the Conservative Party in power.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DOWNING OF IRANIAN AIRLINER BY UNITED STATES NAVAL VESSEL-REQUEST FOR UN EMERGENCY SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. We learned yesterday of the tragic downing of an Iranian airliner in the Persian Gulf. I think I can speak for all Canadians in expressing deep sympathy and regret over this terrible incident. We also recognize that it raises serious questions about further escalation of the conflict in that area and the potential danger this represents to the security of the international aviation system.
In 1983, when we experienced the horrible tragedy of the downing of the Korean airliner, this House unanimously endorsed the actions of the Government, which were to call for an emergency session of the UN Security Council as well as special sessions of the International Civil Aviation organization to investigate the incident and deal with the problems it posed for international aviation. Does the Government intend to take similar measures in this case and ask for an emergency session of the UN Security Council and a special session of ICAO to investigate this terrible and tragic incident?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DOWNING OF IRANIAN AIRLINER BY UNITED STATES NAVAL VESSEL-REQUEST FOR UN EMERGENCY SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada issued a statement and I would like to repeat it.
We learned with shock and profound regret of yesterday's loss of life aboard the Iranian airliner and we extend to the bereaved our deepest sympathy. This tragic event is a grim reminder of the dangers of continued instability in that region. All concerned must recognize the need to pursue with a greater sense of urgency efforts to bring this conflict to an end.
With respect to the incident itself, we have made no decision to take either of the actions which the hon. gentleman mentioned. We will see what the countries immediately involved suggest should be pursued.
The U.S. claims that the aircraft was mistakenly identified as an Iranian F-14 on a direct course with U.S.A. warships which were at the time engaged with five Iranian gunboats which had attacked American forces in the region, and that the Airbus failed to respond to repeated warnings issued by the U.S. vessel on both military and civilian channels.

July 4, 1988
Oral Questions
We were shocked by this but there is no reason at this time to doubt the description of the events as provided by the United States. We will continue to look into this with great interest. We will take a position when we have all the facts.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ACT TO ENSURE IMPARTIAL INVESTIGATION
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ACT TO ENSURE IMPARTIAL INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I asked was on exactly that point, that is, to get the facts, to have a proper inquiry and investigation into all the circumstances surrounding this, based upon the representations of the countries affected the United States, Iran, and other countries in the Persian Gulf.
I do not understand why the Government is not prepared to take action now when we were able to take in 1983. The United Nations was able to respond as was the International Civil Aviation Organization. Proposals were put forward.
Considering the precedent set and the unanimous support it received in this House, why will the Government not take measures to ensure proper, effective, impartial international investigation of this tragic circumstance?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT ACT TO ENSURE IMPARTIAL INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that if we wish to be fair we will see that the circumstances surrounding the Korean incident and those surrounding this most unfortunate incident yesterday in the Gulf are hardly similar. It was difficult to tell, for a number of days, what had happened to the Korean aircraft. There are a large number of dissimilar circumstances.
We will take a position and exercise our responsibilities as members of ICAO or as members of the United Nations if and when the matter comes before either of those bodies. We will then support what seems to be the correct and best course of action to take in the interests of humanity and the interests of Canadians. That is our duty and that is what we will do.
We are not a party immediately involved in this incident. We will do what is best for the international community of nations when this matter comes forward and is brought to the attention of these bodies by the countries immediately involved.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA UNDERTAKE INITIATIVE
REQUEST THAT CANADA UNDERTAKE INITIATIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, does the Minister not believe that the best course of action would be to try to get a resolution of the circumstances and that, rather than being passive and taking no action at all, it would be far more appropriate for Canada, with the reputation which we have in ICAO and in the United Nations, to undertake an initiative before the problem escalates, before there is further retaliation, and before there are further threats and damage to the international civil aviation system?
For the life of me, Mr. Speaker, I do not understand the position of the Government in totally refusing to take positive, constructive action to find out the causes and to put forward
proposals and measures which might prevent these kinds of incidents from happening in the future.
Are we prepared to propose that there be special meetings to investigate? Are we prepared to ask the countries to ratify the amendments of the Chicago Convention which would provide better rules for the interception of civilian aircraft? Why will the Government not take the appropriate action to forestall future escalation of this conflict?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT CANADA UNDERTAKE INITIATIVE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have explained our position and it is a sensible, reasonable, and responsible one. We have no reason to doubt the U.S. version of what occurred yesterday in the Strait of Hormuz.
As members of ICAO and the United Nations we will support whatever responsible action either of those agencies feels it is necessary to take. I believe that Iran has brought this to the attention of ICAO and has asked for an extraordinary session.
We will play our role when the time comes to play that role. In the meantime, we have no reason to doubt that the United States has given a version of the events which is incorrect. There is no evidence that its version is incorrect. I see no similarity between this and the Korean air incident. At that time it was not even admitted by the U.S.S.R. for a number of days that a Korean airliner had disappeared.

Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the crop conditions on the Prairies are very uncertain due to the very severe drought. As a result, the price of grain is very volatile. Certainly, we as a Government have been committed to continuing the policy of trying to ensure that as much of the farmer's money is made available to him up front when he needs it most. In other words, we tried to keep initial prices as high as possible.
If the crop conditions are such and the prices are such that it would seem as if an increase in the initial price would be warranted between now and the beginning of the new crop year, which is about four weeks away, then that announcement will be made as close as possible, I would assume, to the beginning of that new crop year to ensure that the price is accurate.
In the meantime I note, and I think most farmers are already doing this, that what little grain is left on the Prairies is very often being delivered. Storage tickets are being taken out to ensure that if there is to be a higher price in place at the beginning of the new crop year then the farmer would receive that.
I also note that some grain companies apparently are beginning to waive that storage fee as well to assist the farm community.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think mine will be one of the most protracted 10-minute speeches that will have been given in the House. I would now like to return to discussing Bill C-130. I think it has tremendous benefits for all Canadians and, in particular, for those living in Ontario.
Today I would like to take a province-wide perspective. Trade is an issue of considerable importance to Ontario, particularly trade with the United States. Fully 90 per cent of all Ontario's exports go to the U.S. while 83 per cent of this province's imports come from south of the border. That is why the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement is so important for us here in Ontario. We sought an agreement that would secure and enhance our access to the vital U.S. market. We fought hard for Ontario's interests and we have a great deal to show for our efforts. Unfortunately, there is some misunderstanding about this agreement here in Ontario, especially at Queen's Park.
First, David Peterson said he would support free trade but only if certain conditions were met. Then, when those conditions were met, he still said, no, he could not support the agreement. Then he said he was going to do everything he could to fight the deal. Now, he says he will wait and see. As John Diefenbaker once said:
The Liberals are the flying saucers of politics. No one can make head nor
tail of them and they never are seen twice in the same place.
Today, Madam Speaker, I want to set the record straight for the people of Ontario about this agreement, beginning with the automotive provisions.
Naturally the automotive provisions are of keen interest to Ontario where the automotive industry is the largest employer in the province. The Premier has said he worries that the Auto Pact could be gutted. His worries have no basis in fact. From the outset of the negotiations we said that the Auto Pact was working well and that Canada would not raise it. We did not. The Government also said that if the Americans made proposals which offered the potential for more production and employment in Canada, we would listen to them. The Americans did have some ideas which we found to be a sound basis for discussion. The result is what has been described as Auto Pact Plus. We have kept the fundamental elements of the Auto Pact and added provisions in the agreement which will stimulate new opportunities for production and employment in Canada.
Let me be more specific. For Auto Pact producers, not much has changed. They can continue to operate as they have been
and retain their third-country privileges which will now be denied to newcomers. For Canadian parts producers, this is a good package. For sales to the Auto Pact producers, the situation will be unchanged except that vehicles assembled in Canada will have to meet a higher standard of North American content to qualify for duty free entry to the U.S. This is a real incentive to procure high levels of domestic parts.
What about parts producers selling or hoping to sell to the transplants in North America? The rules of origin negotiated in the agreement and the end of the duty drawbacks will create a real incentive for assemblers to increase their sourcing of North American parts to qualify for the reduced tariffs. These are highly positive developments.
Just as positive are the provisions pertaining to agricultural trade. In essence, the agreement provides for agricultural trade a balanced deal which makes important gains for our primary exporters and at the same time safeguards our marketing board system for sensitive sectors such as dairy and eggs. Ontario's beef and meat processing industries will gain from the exemption from U.S. meat import laws. Fruit and vegetable producers will be protected for 20 years by special tariff measures which can be invoked when prices are abnormally low.
With respect to investment, David Peterson has expressed considerable concern about the levels of foreign investment, something which sounds a bit strange coming from the man who has thrown open the Ontario securities industry to foreign takeovers, as economist John Crispo has pointed out. The Premier's concerns are ill-founded. Canada keeps the right to restrict U.S. investment in key sectors such as energy, transportation and culture, we also retain our ability to review major direct acquisitions by non-Canadians.
Those who are defensive about foreign investment forget that Canada is now a major net exporter of capital and has been since 1975. As an importer and exporter of capital, Canada has much to gain from a secure and stable investment environment at home and abroad.
Increased investment is particularly important to northern Ontario's key industries such as mining. New investment means more jobs and more secure jobs, especially for northern Ontarians who make up 73 per cent of the province's mining workforce.
Let me move on to dispute settlement, an issue I hear a lot about in northern Ontario where there is concern about the impact of U.S. protectionism on our forestry and steel exports. As Ambassador Reisman has pointed out, our objective in the area of dispute settlement was to ensure greater certainty about the rules of the game. What we have achieved is binding objectivity in the application of anti-dump and countervail laws by both parties.
The dispute settlement provisions make Canada an equal partner in the resolution of disputes and provide for fair and effective solutions to difficult problems. Canadians will know
July 4, 1988

what the rules are and can be confident that they will have a voice in how they will be applied. How can anyone claim that this is not an improvement over what we have now?
For Ontario's service industries, there is also good news. The agreement will ensure that Canadian service businesses can compete with U.S. companies on an equal footing. Our entrepreneurs and businesses will have easier access to the U.S. to sell their goods and services and to supply after-sales service to their customers. This alone is a very practical achievement for Ontario with its large service sector.
With respect to financial services, the agreement promotes the Government's policy objectives for this sector that were set out last December. Those objectives are to increase competition, innovation and efficiency, to broaden sources of credit and options for consumers and to promote international competitiveness and domestic growth.
The agreement will open up a major new area of the securities market for Canadian banks in the U.S. At the same time, we retain the right to control entry of foreign banks into our financial markets and we keep full power to regulate chartered financial institutions operating in Canada.
What about jobs and free trade? Free trade critics claim that there will be many job losses. This is not so according to the Economic Council and the Conference Board, both of which predict increased employment as a result of free trade.
With respect to jobs and women, the Economic Council forecasts that half the new jobs created by this agreement will be in the retail and wholesale trade and in the commercial, personal care and business services. This is very favourable for Canadian women because 84 per cent of Canadian women work in service industries. The C. D. Howe Institute also agrees. It says that since women hold more than half the jobs in the services sector, they are well positioned to benefit from this employment expansion.
What about labour adjustment, another issue which has been brought up on numerous occasions? Critics ignore the fact that adjustment due to free trade will be small compared to normal labour adjustment that occurs each year in our economy. They also ignore the fact that the Government already has in place a wide array of labour adjustment programs. In addition, we have established the Advisory Council on Adjustment which will make an interim report this summer on the adequacy of existing programs.
An example that will need assistance is Ontario's grape and wine sectors which will need to adjust not just to free trade but also to the recent GATT panel ruling. Since December, we have been consulting extensively with provincial officials and the industry on an assistance package for these sectors.
Today, I repeat this challenge. I ask all the enterprising people of Ontario to help us take Canada forward to greater economic growth and prosperity for our sons and daughters.
Time Allocation

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is difficult for Canadians listening to the debates to know where the exaggerations are on both sides of the House.
I myself have had great difficulty understanding the issues in this debate. Canadians are entitled to know why the Government has gagged the Opposition in the House of Commons during the free trade debate. This is the most important Bill before Parliament in the 121 years since Confederation.
Canada's independence and sovereignty are at stake in Bill C-130. We should start by solving our interprovincial problems before getting into free trade with the United States.
A construction worker from Ontario cannot work in the Province of Quebec. We do not even have free movement between the provinces of Canada. For example, professional associations and corporations are under provincial jurisdiction in Canada and state jurisdiction in the United States. We know that the professional corporations in Quebec have very strict prerequisites with which professionals from other provinces must comply if they come to Quebec. We also know that the Americans' prerequisites are less strict and exacting. So we wonder what kind of services we will have in Canada after free trade with the Americans. Are we ready to lower the quality of our services, are we prepared to decrease the health protection of Canadian patients? There are many other imponderables in this Accord. Many decisions will depend on the interpretation given to it. For example, in future, will we need American approval before deciding whether a Government can nationalize automobile insurance, as has been done in Quebec and Saskatchewan?
There are already several other irritants between Canada and the United States. For example, the Americans steadfastly refuse to admit they are partially responsible for acid rain, an environmental issue which could be the subject of long debates.
Hon. Members will recall as well that we lost the fight over Arctic waters sovereignty in 1985, particularly the stealthy saga of the American icebreaker Polar Sea. Mr. Reagan laughed in our Prime Minister's face (Mr. Mulroney) by having him sign the Arctic co-operation agreement. Just what is the meaning of a co-operation agreement? It means that the Americans are stubborn and that under no consideration whatsoever will they acknowledge our sovereignty in the Arctic waters and the Northwest Passage.
Signing the agreement was tantamount to the Conservative Government's admission of being powerless to control the ongoing activities of the American giant in the Far North.
Conservative publicity would have us believe that we are looking at the perfect recipe for happiness, a recipe which is being sold to the Canadian public just like a fairy tale we tell our children. Everything is beautiful, everything is fine, not to worry, everything eventually will turn out all right. No way!

July 4, 1988
Time Allocation
Before going any further I want to make sure that Canadians who are listening realize that the Official Opposition is not against free trade, we are simply against this agreement bearing the signatures of Mulroney and Reagan.
Since the end of World War II the Liberal Party in office has always negotiated freer trade through GATT. It did so successfully and to the advantage of Canada. Nothing prevents Canada from continuing and even improving this kind of negotiations.
My leader, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner), stated in his speech on free trade that this agreement represents the largest sell-out of our sovereignty since we became a nation. He went on to say that with this agreement we are losing the ability and power to govern our own country, to choose our policies and to fulfill our national destiny as Canadians.
The Conservatives want us to believe that a general agreement with the United States is more advantageous because it would guarantee access to the huge American market. But, Madam Speaker, we already have access to a major part of the American market.
Since its creation in 1947 GATT paved the way for tariff reductions-then 40 per cent on average-to an average rate of 5 per cent now. Roughly 80 per cent of those products are already being exported duty-free to the United States. To put it another way, the Mulroney-Reagan general trade agreement is aimed at guaranteeing access to the rest of the market, only 20 per cent. That is clear enough!
The question is this: Does the agreement we have on the table guarantee the access the Conservatives have been striving to achieve? The answer is no, and there are three reasons for that. Last month the American Congress passed its omnibus bill, and henceforth this legislation will impose additional tariffs on all countries exporting to the United States, including Canada. Yet President Reagan had promised to veto this omnibus bill personally to protect Canada. He has yet to deliver and chances are we will face new tariff barriers on January 1, 1989 when the free trade agreement comes into force.
Furthermore, elements of this omnibus bill will be part of the next GATT negotiations. We will therefore not have access to these markets and we will have to renegotiate these items at the next round of GATT when we will already be bound by the Free Trade Agreement.
Second, the dispute settlement mechanism is deficient because we will be subject to U.S. laws.
Gordon Ritchie, ambassador and deputy chief negotiator at the Canadian Trade Netgotiations Office, admitted to the House of Commons Committee that Canada had not obtained any guaranteed access. According to him, U.S. law will continue to apply in this area. The Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) pointed out to us that Article 1902(1) of the Agreement specifies that the United States
reserves the right to apply its own legislation, its laws on antidumping and countervailing duties, to all products imported from the territory of the other party, namely Canada.
In the case of potash, steel and lumber, we have already paid the price.
Third, the dispute settlement mechanism is wanting. The three panels have no authority to enforce this Agreement.
It is mainly for these three reasons that we do not agree with this Agreement.
First, President Reagan has not yet exempted us from the U.S. omnibus trade bill; second, we are subject to American laws and third, the dispute settlement mechanism is ineffective.
Also, in the field for which I am a critic, the dispute on Class "C" plywood, which is of superior quality in Canada, and Class "D", which is an inferior U.S. quality, is a problem for Canada even before the Agreement takes effect. Although Canada offered to develop a test for the strength of Canadian plywood, the Americans still refuse to submit to it.
This dispute will particularly affect construction of public housing. The Americans are making a big issue of it and want us Canadians to lower the quality of our plywood. There is no question of Americans improving the quality of theirs. It is not as unimportant as it may seem because it shows what will happen every time the Americans want to have access to our Canadian market.
This can have serious consequences for public housing. For example, we have often heard very heated debates in this House when Members exposed the deplorable conditions of housing for native people in Canada.
Houses on reservations last about 15 years. If we lower the quality of the plywood used in building them, we are likely to have to replace them much sooner.
Public housing, which as we know is partly subsidized by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, will also be greatly affected by this U.S. decision. The Conservatives well know that I am watching them on this issue. I have made statements in the House, I have questioned the Minister responsible for housing and I do think that the Americans and the Government will pay attention, but we will have to keep on the lookout during the vacation period. It is very easy to have the wool pulled over you, as happened to Quebec, during the vacation period.
