speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we now have before the House a motion that will allow us to vote on a matter of vital importance to western Canada. We have heard much in this debate about free trade and its short-term impact on Canadian consumers, businesses and workers. We
July 4, 1988

have heard from those who want to promote Canada to the world and those who want to remove Canada from the world. I want to consider the free trade agreement in light of the long term opportunities it presents, especially for western Canada, and the step forward in global relations that it represents.
Free trade resolves at least one problem which has plagued western Canada for a century and responds to the future challenges the whole country will face. Ever since John A. Macdonald's national policy the tariff system in Canada has worked to the disadvantage of western Canada. We sold our products on the international market at low prices but had to buy goods on the highly protected domestic one. Free trade is about to change that imbalance.
With free trade, western businesses will continue to compete as they have all along and western consumers will have the advantage of access to tariff-free imports from the United States. We can look forward to a revitalized economy, modernization, and real income growth. No wonder Albertans are among the strongest supporters of free trade!
At the First Ministers' Conference on the economy in February, 1985, former Premier Peter Lougheed of Alberta presented his belief that free trade would create jobs and opportunities for Canadians, hie had supported the idea at the 1977 Premiers of Canada Conferences and it was supported again in the provincial Government White Paper on Industrial and Science Strategy. This time, though, the federal Government gave some consideration to western ideas.
What was being suggested was a mutually beneficial package of reductions in tariff and non-tariff barriers and that is what has been negotiated. I cannot say that westerners are totally responsible for bringing about the free trade agreement, but former Premier Lougheed was certainly instrumental in getting it placed on the national agenda. I think it is a credit to the current Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) that he has pursued the matter.
At the 1985 First Ministers' Conference it was stated that: "From Alberta's perspective, a free trade arrangement is a viable method of overcoming obstacles to the revitalization of our economy. The benefits from expanded trade, the effect on industrial restructuring, rationalization, modernization, technological enhancement, productivity improvement, and real income growth can be realized if a free trade agreement is put into place ... Federal and provincial Governments must now demonstrate their leadership and show that Canada has the self-confidence and political maturity to pursue a free trade arrangement with the United States".
The Alberta Government was saying then, and I am repeating now, that free trade is crucial for the economic future of the West, and, for that matter, all of Canada. It is also an indicator of the future economic policies that Canada must pursue. Canada dare not complacently accept the status
Time Allocation
quo. We must consider our own style of perestroika, our own methods of securing economic well-being into the future.
U.S. Secretary of State George Shultz spoke before the World Affairs Council in late 1987. He briefly mentioned some of the changes that he saw under way in technology, artificial intelligence, genetic engineering, and language. He concluded his overview with the comment that "in this time of profound change one of the hardest adjustments to make is intellectual adjustment. We must discard outdated habits of thinking and make room for new possibilities ..."
We must consider that we are working today in measures of speed and magnitude that were only dreamt about a few years ago. Money now moves in international markets as quickly as it can be electronically relayed. We are using substances that were invented yesterday, not only resources that have been with us since the Earth was formed. Information changes as quickly as we can read it. These changes have implications on how we conduct our lives and how we must manage our governments.
Secretary Shultz suggested that countries which cannot or will not compete in the global market-place and interact with ideas from other societies will find themselves falling behind the advanced innovators and producers. Some may absorb these changes and benefit in a small way, others will simply become marginal. Free trade is only the first of many steps that Canada must take to meet the challenges of sharing ideas, coping with change, and being competitive enough to maintain our standard of living.
All countries face challenges, not only Canada. All are looking for solutions. It only follows that other countries have displayed an interest in our free trade agreement and have considered it as a model.
Members will recall the media controversy about the comments of British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher when she spoke in this Chamber. Putting that controversy aside, I believe it is important to consider what she said and what it implies. The United Kingdom is our third largest trading partner, so she knows that Canadians can compete in the European market. She referred to the fact that Canada, with less than 1 per cent of the world's population, accounts for 5 per cent of its trade. On the basis of her country's experience within the European Economic Community, Prime Minister Thatcher applauded the agreement and the example it sets for other trading nations.
The free trade agreement is part of the Government's strategy to ensure Canada's continued success into the 21st century. It will increase Canadian business opportunities, make it easier for professionals to work on both sides of the border, and lower consumer prices for everyone. The free trade agreement is a triumph for the open market in Canada.
The free market cannot operate with stifling regulation, interference, or political difficulties. That is why our Government's policies, like decentralization, privatization, and

July 4, 1988
Time Allocation
deregulation, have brought increased employment, investment, and record economic growth.
The socialists do not share the view that Canadian businesses can grow with increased market opportunities or that Canadian workers are skilled enough to compete. A few days ago we heard in this Chamber from Chancellor Kohl of West Germany who also spoke of the importance of trade and freer trade. He should know. West Germany is one of the most powerful economies in the world and has the highest percentage of Gross National Product dependent on external trade of all the industrialized countries. Canada is second. West Germany provides a valuable model with its expanding economy and stable position in the OECD.
The East German economy, on the other hand, is restricted by government control, enforced isolation, inefficiency, and a far lower standard of living. We, of course, are favouring the first; the socialists would have us adopt the second.
The socialists are wrong on two counts. First, they have assumed that independence is the ability to go it alone. This is a grave error. The independence of nations is not based on their protectionism or their retrenchment. It is based on their ability to assert themselves on the world stage, their ability to command international respect for their policies and actions. We are proud of leaders, not of hermits.
Second, the socialists have forgotten that education, transportation, communications, and technology are the determinants of the economy. Markets, not governments, determine economic results and there is no way to overrule the market more than momentarily in an age when goods, services, capital and technology flow across international boundaries.
The free trade agreement will provide the mechanism for open trade with the Americans. Beyond that is the fact that global economic power has been dispersing. Ours is no longer a bi-polar world with the United States and the U.S.S.R. determining military policy and economic conditions. Developing countries like Brazil, Korea, China, India and Israel have become important commercial powers. In this new environment it is important to remember that we are trading as parts of blocs, not as individual nations.
Europe is one market, so is the Pacific Rim. We must consider our place within our own corner of the globe then look outward for other opportunities.
We must also remember what Montesquieu said more than 200 years ago for I believe that it is still true.
[ Translation]
The natural effect of trade is to lead to peace. Two nations that negotiate together become mutually dependent; one wishes to buy, the other wishes to sell; thus, all unions are based on mutual need."

The natural effect of commerce is to lead to peace. In other words, our movement toward global trade can be an important
step toward world peace. With a free trade agreement we have established our role within the North American economic unit. We have chosen to compete with the Americans on an equal basis. We are choosing to be active participants in this quickly changing world. This choice will make us better businesspeople, better workers, and better Canadians.

Madam Speaker, I know that I have only a short period of time and I want to make sure that I fill it with a lot of punch. I remind the House that we are debating a motion of the Conservative Government to stop dead in its tracks the debate in principle on Bill C-130 which Simon Reisman called the greatest deal of the century. Simon Reisman, the negotiator of the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal, said it was the great deal of the century. After two and one half days of debate the Government has brought forward a motion to stop debate dead in its tracks, to guillotine the debate.
What are the Tories afraid of? Are they afraid of the Opposition? No, I do not think so, they are 200 strong. Are they afraid of the Speaker? No, they are not afraid of the Speaker.
I will tell you who they are afraid of. They are afraid of the Canadian people. They know that Canadians would find out more about this deal through debate that would be coming to them on prime time television with the extended hours of the House. The Tories cannot stand the scrutiny of this Bill. This paltry, porous proposal of the Tories will not stand up to the scrutiny of a vigilant opposition. That is why they have come to close the debate. What a shameful performance.
Let us look at the history of this infamous Bill. First we have the man who signed for Colonel McCormick for $5, singing When Irish Eyes are Smiling, in Quebec City for his American boss. They cooked up this deal.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has exhibited himself to be nothing but a lackey for the American power in Washington. He has switched from Colonel McCormick to Colonel Reagan.
We had the inimitable Solicitor General (Mr. Kelleher), formerly Minister for International Trade. Of course, they did not want that Minister handling international trade so it was put into the hands of that character from Dick and Jane. When the appointment was made the Prime Minister said: "I have given the ball to Pat. Watch Pat go. See Pat go. Jump Pat, jump. Run Pat, run." The Americans simply held up the hoop and said how high.
We were given an incongruous image of midnight approaching as the deal must be signed. Thank God Simon was not working overtime at $1,000 a day. As midnight was approaching, where was the Minister? She was on the beaches of Waikiki, unable to be there. What a mess. The former

Minister for International Trade was not there when she was needed the most. She was on the beach at Waikiki.
The Prime Minister took that portfolio from the Minister and gave it to the new Willy Loman of the Conservative Cabinet, the man who could not sell vacuum cleaners.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the Conservative Party was elected to office in 1984 our commitment as a new Government was to undo the damage of the past. We were left with a 20 year Liberal legacy of spiralling government spending, federal-provincial squabbles, squandered economic opportunities and a devalued economy.
During that election campaign we said that we would bring the country together so that we could meet the challenge of change. We said we would fight poverty and unemployment in the only way they can be effectively fought, by creating a stable economic environment, by creating growth and investment, and by creating jobs. We said that we would restore Canada's reputation to what it had been before as an active and reliable participant in global affairs, securely from the positions as a reliable member of the western alliance. All of this has been done, Madam Speaker.
Despite the most dire predictions of the Opposition, Canada is in better shape than it has been for decades. But that fact has not stopped the critics and the naysayers. These same people said that our economic policies introduced in 1984-85 would cost hundreds of thousands of Canadians their jobs. They were wrong. Instead, more than one million new jobs have been created since 1984. Those same people today in the Opposition say that free trade threatens our very existence as a people and a nation. They will be proved wrong once again.
The opponents of free trade have, to date, fought this initiative not through engaging the federal Government in debate on the merits of what the agreement contains, but by raising the spectre of dangers that do not exist, a process that is designed to confuse and to scare the public. Today I join this debate to outline the benefits of free trade to the region and to the people I know best, those of eastern Ontario.
Let me place this latest initiative in its true context. The last time Canada was faced with a free trade debate was in 1911. If we had got together then at some town hall meeting, we would have all arrived by horse and buggy and everyone would have learned of the meeting by newspaper or word of mouth since telephones at that time were not in wide use. In short, we lived in a different world. We now live in a world of satellites and instant communications where decisions taken across an ocean may affect our business dealings the same day.
Where does Canada fit into this modern world? We fit in as the odd man out. Canada is a trading nation but it is in a world of trading blocs. To the south lies the United States of America, 50 states in one economic union with a population of 260 million people. It is a trading bloc unto itself. Second, there is the European Economic Community, which is comprised of 16 nations with a total population of 320 million people. Third, there is Japan and the Pacific Rim nations with hundreds of millions of people. Fourth, the Soviet bloc countries have their own trading organization known as Comecon. Fifth, Brazil and Argentina signed a free trade
agreement earlier this year. Sixth, Australia and New Zealand have recently gone into a free trade agreement. Then there is Canada with 25 million people dependent on trade for prosperity, but we are not a member of any trading bloc, thus we have no leverage, no protection and, yes, we are vulnerable.
We are vulnerable to the wars between the trading blocs. The United States has already demonstrated that with the grain price war. Also we are vulnerable to action taken against us by trading blocs. The United States Congress proved that when it turned protectionist. Industries like softwood lumber, shakes and shingles, hogs and steel suffered severe damage and heavy losses. Many companies went bankrupt. Worse still, workers lost their jobs.
The opponents of free trade say we should stick with the status quo. The examples of the last two years have shown that that is really not a true option. Opponents of the free trade agreement say we will lose our sovereignty. It was only a week ago that Prime Minister Thatcher addressed this House and observed that concerns about our cultural sovereignty were unfounded, just as those same concerns on the part of some of her countrymen about EEC membership were proven unfounded.
Our critics say that this comparison will not work, that we are too small, that the U.S. neighbour is too big. I say to them that the island of the United Kingdom had a free trade agreement before it joined the European Economic Community. Were the Irish ever less sovereign? Were they less Irish because of it? I think not, Madam Speaker. After England joined the European Economic Community, did it lose its sovereignty? Is Maggie Thatcher not the Prime Minister of an independent country? Isn't Queen Elizabeth the sovereign Queen of an independent state? For that matter, look at Australia and New Zealand. They signed a free trade agreement to be phased in over 10 years. It worked so well that the process was shortened to a six-year period. Are New Zealanders any less sovereign? Did the agreement keep New Zealand from taking a radically different international position from Australia on the issue of nuclear arms on visiting U.S. nuclear-powered warships?
We have been working toward freer trade for some 40 years. At the end of the Second World War, the average tariffs in this country were 35 per cent. Today, where tariffs apply at all, the average is 9 per cent or 10 per cent. Eighty per cent of our trade with the United States is already duty free. Trade barriers have been steadily lowered for decades. Is Canada less sovereign because of that? Have Canadians lost jobs because of that? Of course not. In fact, in that period of time we have become more prosperous. This free trade agreement really just completes the process. It phases our the remaining tariffs with the United States over the next 10 years.
When our Government embarked on negotiating freer trade with the United States it was understood that Canada, and all its regions, depends on trade for its prosperity. We set out to achieve a bilateral agreement with the United States, our
July 4, 1988

largest trading partner, while at the same time pursuing global negotiations and initiatives. In fact, if we do not like the free trade deal with the United States after trying it, then the ultimate act of sovereignty is to cancel it, and we can do so with a mere six months' notice.
In my view the free trade agreement negotiated with the United States presents eastern Ontario with its greatest opportunity ever to catch up with other parts of the province in our manufacturing sector and in getting our share of the high quality, high skilled jobs which our children seek as their future career choices, their future career options. That is the message I am hearing from business, from professionals and from academics in my region, the people who understand what the vocal opponents of free trade do not, that in this modern world there are linkages between trade, technology and investment which are the keys to job creation.
In my own federal riding of Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton my office surveyed 155 manufacturers. Some 68 per cent of the respondents favoured an agreement with the United States which would eliminate tariffs and reduce other trade barriers to the flow of goods and services between both countries. I believe that free trade is Canada's best best bet for greater diversification and more growth. I ask the people to consider those remarks. I do so because I believe the greatest danger to our Canadian way of life lies not in the prosperity of free trade, but in the poverty of protectionism. If we fail to go forth to expand, to progress, then we will not be able to afford the regional development, the social and cultural programs which are a reality and reflect Canadian values.
I do not have to tell you, Madam Speaker, that the Great Depression of the 1930s started with a stock market crash, but far fewer people understand that the Depression lasted a decade because of short-sighted trade protectionism around the world. Should we turn and run from the opportunities of freer trade? If we choose to retreat behind protectionist walls, I fear we could repeat the mistakes of the past and suffer the consequences.
I am as dedicated a Canadian nationalist as anyone. I believe that the freer trade agreement is the only path to follow to ensure the economic future of my region, in this province and in this country. That is why in the end I am confident that after this debate it is not the shrill negative voices of our critics that will prevail but, rather, the common sense of Canadians who have decided on its merits that this important economic opportunity must be pursued.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House to express my astonishment and indeed embarrassment at the Government's decision to end the debate on the Mul-roney-Reagan agreement. I am, as they say in English, appalled at the way the Government has dealt with the impact on women, when we know that this particular group stands to
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
lose the most. Since the Conservative Government came to power, its members have said constantly that giving women their rightful place was one of their priorities. But look at what this Government is doing, and look at this agreement: sadly, the Mulroney-Reagan agreement contains no protection for women and minorities.
For instance, we know that 63 per cent of workers in the service industries are women, and Canada not only has to compete with the U.S. but also with developing countries that will produce and are in fact producing and exporting goods at far lower cost. Many women who work in the services industry have little education. Many are immigrants who speak neither English nor French. If these women lose their jobs, they will have a hard time finding other jobs because it is very likely no retraining will be provided in the services sector. We have asked the Government many times to include this as one of the conditions for the service sector, so that women can retrain for other jobs, especially when we realize that over 65 per cent of single-parent families are headed by women, who in that case are the sole breadwinner. Of course this Government has always refused to commit itself. I would like to quote from a study prepared in Ontario.

In the Ontario study it indicated that 44 per cent of women's jobs in manufacturing will be vulnerable under free trade. That works out to 100,000 jobs being lost. A Quebec study estimated that at least 30,000 jobs in Quebec would be in jeopardy. The job loss could be due to several things. First, the manufacturing industry in Canada is dominated by American subsidiaries. Once the U.S. has access to our markets it will take companies out of Canada to areas where labour is cheaper and where there are fewer labour standards.
Second, as pressure is raised on businesses to cut costs and become competitive under free trade many companies will replace jobs with high technology. This rationalization of production will mean heavy job losses for women.
Within the service industry the impact of women's jobs will be even greater. For services that are international, that is, banking, telecommunications, education, health, accounting and others, women make up 82 per cent of the labour force. Canada's economy is a service economy. We rely on the service sector to generate jobs and to increase our GNP. Services account for two thirds of the national income and provide 70 per cent of jobs in Canada.
Moreover, historically free trade agreements, such as the GATT, have had as their focus the liberalization of trade in merchandise and have not dealt with liberalizing trade in the service industry. The important point here with respect to services is that we have not yet defined what services will be affected by the trade agreement. This service industry might include such things as medical care and child care and thus will affect women as consumers and as employees within those industries.

We know that today, daycare is one of our priorities in Canada and that the Conservative Government has said it is committed to tabling a child care program before the next election. This is probably one of the services that will be affected by the agreement. Today, American companies are sending us proposals for establishing daycare services in the provinces, especially in the West. I know what I am talking about because I have copies of letters, asking me what I thought and whether I would agree to approve their projects. So in some provinces we are going to see a series of daycare centres run by American companies, centres that will not be subject to Canadian regulations and that will be able to operate, whatever the Government of Canada may decide to do. Madam Speaker, I object to this approach because I don't think we can treat daycare centres like some kind of McDonald chain, because children are much too important for that. This is one of the services where standards will not be observed, and where the emphasis will be on operating daycare centres at a profit. I don't think children should be used to make money.
This is only the tip of the iceberg. The social services sector includes services that would take care of handicapped children and children who are mentally disturbed. There would also be homes for single mothers. There are not many of these today. And it also includes ambulance services and rehabilitation clinics. If private companies are asked to operate these services, well, private services are often less accessible and far more expensive. Fewer people would have access, and we would have two classes of Canadians, like the present situation in the United States.
I was invited by the U.S. Government on a three week tour in 1984, to take a look at the women's programs and other programs set up by the Reagan administration. I later wrote to the President to say that I appreciated the trip, but that since he was elected, there were far more elderly people, including women, sleeping on the sidewalks; that all job retraining programs for women had been cut and that his record in this respect was pretty poor.
So we really have to do something, and this is one of the reasons why I am totally against free trade, because I get the impression that Mr. Reagan is the one who will be calling the shots.

The United States has challenged many Canadian Government programs claiming that they are barriers to trade. These include unemployment insurance, subsidized business, regional development and tax incentives. The pressure will be on the Canadian Government to stop intervening and let market forces prevail. This could prevent any kind of affirmative action programs focused on encouraging equity in employment by means of tax relief. It could also, and will undoubtedly, preclude industrial training programs which now benefit women. It will challenge the extension of maternity benefits
through unemployment insurance as an unfair subsidy to employers.

Madam Speaker, we know that maternity leave is not granted automatically in the United States and that this is left up to each employer, whereas in Canada, mothers are granted a minimum number of weeks off, and we are attempting to obtain parental leave as well. And so this is totally unacceptable.
Madam Speaker, I protest, and I have this to say to the Government. If free trade is as important as the Government says it is, it absolutely cannot conclude such an agreement without having done something quite specific for women, who make up 52 per cent of the population. And, at this time, I find the Conservative Government's approach to women and employment in Canada totally unacceptable. Let me reiterate that is is totally unacceptable! Furthermore, I am asking Canadian women to remember this, since we are heading for an election, and to remember how the Conservative Government handled their priorities.

This free trade agreement is of such historic importance to Canada that, regardless of which side one is on in the debate, we should debate it thoroughly, comprehensively and for however long it takes to cover the document without rushing it through. I would have thought that we should have continued the debate, even if for no reason other than to give the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), the Minister who is in charge of selling the sell-out of Canada, the opportunity to read the document. Perhaps, having read it, he might change his mind about the quality of the document.
The question I want to focus on is whether or not there is anything to fear with regard to the free trade agreement that our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has made with the American President.

I want to raise that question because of what I have heard from my hon. friend across the way. We in the Opposition have been accused of raising fears unnecessarily, of playing to the fears of people without cause. The Government has been using that line to try to convince people to rest easy about the free trade agreement. Government Members have
July 4, 1988

said that it is just the Opposition raising unfounded fears while in fact what we have is a deal that is great for Canada.
Not only have government Members been saying this but they have been putting these words in the mouths of other world leaders. They attempted to use the Economic Summit to sell their sell-out of Canada. Of course, they got the full cooperation of the Prime Minister of Great Britain, Margaret Thatcher.
Mrs. Thatcher came before this Chamber and said to Canadians: "You have nothing to fear from free trade, it will do you nothing but good, it will not harm your identity whatsoever". She said in Canada that there is nothing to fear from the harmonization of policies with the Americans, from having closer economic links with the Americans. She said that there will be nothing but prosperity ahead of us and that we have nothing to fear.
What happened once Mrs. Thatcher went home? What happened to the Iron Lady when she got back to Britain? She was under pressure from the European Economic Community to co-ordinate her policies more closely with those of the European Economic Community, to establish a central European bank and to turn over the British central bank to the European Economic Community. What did she say to that? Did she tell the people of Britain that they have nothing to fear, this will bring them greater prosperity, let us make this great leap of faith? That is what she told Canadians, but when she got home to Britain, she told her own people that she said no to having a European central bank.
As far as I know, Mrs. Thatcher did not explain in any great detail why she said no to that, but an official of her Government said quite clearly that if Britain were to agree to this greater harmonization of economic policies with Europe and to the creation of a central bank of Europe, they would first have to give up the British House of Commons because the British House of Commons would be stripped of its power to direct the British economy.

I hear the Tory puppies whimpering over there, saying that that is not in the free trade agreement. Of course, there is no present policy in the free trade agreement providing for a central bank between Canada and the United States, but the policy direction is the same. The direction is toward the harmonization of economic policies. In fact, every Canadian knows that it is a very rare occasion on which our central bank follows a different interest rate policy than that of the United States Federal Reserve. We already have a de facto lock-step branch plant central bank. We are already marching in harmony with the Americans when it comes to monetary policy.
The point I am making is that Mrs. Thatcher sings two tunes. She sings a tune of praise for free trade when in Canada. She tells us that we do not have to worry about the
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
sovereignty of our country or about the powers of Parliament, we will continue to have plenary powers and there is nothing to fear. However, when she turns her back on us and goes back to Britain and is faced with demands from the European Economic Community, she says no because she knows that to acquiesce to such demands means a weakening, an undercutting, a sabotaging of the powers of the British Parliament. She is asking Canadians to accept a weaker House of Commons, a diluted House of Commons, while she herself will not put up with that.
Mrs. Thatcher reassured us that, based on her experience with the European Economic Community, Canada has nothing to fear from entering into a deal with the United States. Yet even the Iron Lady is being forced to succumb. While she was saying no to a European central bank, to a weakening of the British House of Commons, she was forced to acquiesce to a request to become part of a committee studying how to coordinate the monetary policies of Europe and of Great Britain, a first step down the road to a European central bank. It is first step down the road to weakening the British House of Commons. Even the Iron Lady has been forced by the pressures of entering into this kind of deal to move in a direction that will eventually weaken and sabotage the British House of Commons.
We know that we in this country have no assurance of having a Prime Minister who has the courage to stand up for principle and to stand up to foreign adversaries. We have someone who offers a smile to every slap in the face.
The point I want to make is that Canadians have good reason to be concerned about the deal that our Prime Minister has made with the United States. The reassurances of Margaret Thatcher aside, these fears are based on a sound analysis of the free trade agreement. When it comes to investment, this House is giving up the power to set a policy for screening foreign investment, a screening which would see whether or not the foreign investment is to the benefit of Canada. We are being asked to give up the powers of this House to do that under the free trade agreement. At the same time, the Americans are suddenly becoming concerned about foreign investment and are considering policies for screening, controlling and evaluating the benefits of foreign investment in their economy. The Americans are going to be raising their heads when it comes to questioning foreign investment and our hands are going to be tied behind our backs because of this agreement. All of this without an opportunity for the Canadian people to say whether or not they agree with the Government that the agreement is good for Canada, or they agree with the Opposition that there are real grounds for concern and the agreement ought to be put aside and some other more effective way found to regulate our trading relationship with the Americans.
All this agreement has led to is what Mrs. Thatcher said it would not lead to, a weakening of this House of Commons. We

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to enter this debate on the importance of the free trade initiative. First, I would like to comment on some of the things that have just been said, especially with respect to centralized banking. Nothing like that is even talked about in the agreement. The Hon. Member talked about not reading the agreement. I have a feeling that perhaps he did not have the opportunity to read the agreement. One of the reasons we wanted the agreement was so that we could secure our access to the American market for investment by Canadians as well as investment by Americans in our country.
1 would like to speak today about Sarnia-Lambton as it is affected by the agreement. That is an area very important to me, of course, because that is where I come from. It is the petrochemical centre of the east, and so this agreement is very important to us. The petroleum refining and petrochemical industry accounts for over 50 per cent of all employment in that area. I would like to quote from a statement made by Bill McCagherty, a Vice-President of Dow Chemical of Canada, which has its headquarters in Sarnia-Lambton. He said:
We would be hard to beat. Sarnia has an ample supply of feedstocks, a
highly skilled labour force and a competitive energy position. Unobstructed
access to the large, adjacent U.S. market will lead to expansion.
What could be more positive in our area than expansion? It will make available more jobs to our young people graduating from university.
Sarnia-Lambton chemical valley is efficient, world scale and competitive. The industry has supported broad tariff removal with the U.S. for many years. U.S. import tariffs on petrochemicals range as high as 18 per cent, and have been a major impediment to our industry's ability to expand. Under the FTA, both U.S. and Canadian petrochemical tariffs will be phased out over a five to ten-year period. That is important and everyone across the country knows it. The industry was ecstatic. They thought that if we got an agreement to get those tariffs down in ten years we would be doing a great job.
The proximity of the industry to its major customers in Canada and the United States, and the supplier-consumer relations established over many years, will reduce the potential impact of increased competition from the U.S. gulf coast producers.
Ontario is Canada's second largest producer of petrochemicals after Alberta, accounting for 35 per cent of Canadian productive capacity. Since oil and gas represent up to 70 per cent of the cost of petrochemical production, availability and pricing are of critical importance to the industry. Tariffs of 7.5 per cent to 18 per cent are a significant factor in the Canada-U.S. petrochemical trade. Traditionally, the more upgraded the product in Canada, the higher the U.S. tariff. Some Hon.
Member opposite said that under GATT these tariffs would be removed in the year 2000 or so. I tell him that those tariffs in existence today are troublesome to us because they involve downstream type of work, and a real example of that is the petrochemical industry.
The Leaders of both Opposition Parties have talked about tearing up this agreement. Imagine the importance of this industry in both Sarnia-Lambton and in Alberta. Think of the jobs. The tariff on the industry's products is 17.5 per cent now. There is a five-year countdown for removal of that tariff, so 20 per cent of it will have been removed in the first year. The opposition Parties are going to tear up the agreement and tell the petrochemical industry in Canada, "we are going to raise your prices so that you are less competitive in the American market". Imagine what would happen. That illustrates the ridiculous aspect of this threat to tear up the agreement.
This agreement is so good for Sarnia-Lambton that I want to read another statement, and I think the entire House will be interested in this. It is this:
I think that we feel there are some winners in the free trade agreement and I would think that the petrochemical industry is one.
Let me tell you who said that. It was Monte Kwinter, the provincial Industry Minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL OF SECTION 17
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as my colleague from Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) has indicated, there are essentially two kinds of remission orders.
First, there are a few tariff remission orders of substantial dollar value whose purpose is to promote specific industrial developments. Such duty remissions are given conditional on firms meeting performance requirements with respect to investment, production or employment in Canada.
Use of remission orders in this manner might be called the equivalent of a "program". The purposes of such programs will be examined subsequently by one of my colleagues. I might mention, however, that as a result of the free trade agreement, no new remission programs conditional on performance can be introduced after June 30 of this year or after the agreement is approved by the U.S. Congress, whichever comes later, and existing programs of this type must be terminated before 1988.
I propose to examine the other major use of remission orders- in their functions as a fair and timely remedy. I might call the attention of the House to the fact that this is the reason why most remission orders have been granted over the years.
My argument will be that remissions for timely and equitable relief fulfill a useful and necessary function in our tax and tariff systems. Any reasonable system needs a "remedy of last resort" of this kind. I would also submit that the motion of the Member for York East would defeat the purpose of this useful instrument.
Financial Administration Act
Remission orders to deal with unfairness usually come from two sources, Madam Speaker, corresponding to ministerial responsibilities. The Minister of Finance has the responsibility for tax and tariff policy. In the last six months, he sponsored or co-sponsored a total of two tax remission orders-on the grounds that failing to remedy the problems in question would have offended against the principles of a good tax system. In one case, double taxation was involved. In the other case, retroactive taxation would have been involved as a result of a change in legislation.
The vast majority of remissions on grounds of fairness, however, arise in the administration of the tax and tariff system and are sponsored by the Minister of National Revenue. These orders deal with cases of hardship, administrative error, anomalies and unreasonable applications of tax laws or the Customs Tariff.
As Members will know, a taxpayer is barred by statute from claiming relief for an error in filing taxes if the period in which amended returns can be submitted has expired. Remission orders are occasionally given where extreme hardship results or the circumstances were beyond the control of the taxpayer.
A case from the 1986 Public Accounts illustrates the process, Madam Speaker. The recipient of PC 1985-2/3341 was an Iranian resident who was, at the relevant time, prohibited from leaving Iran and was unable to communicate with anyone in Canada since it was dangerous for Iranians to own property outside of Iran. One can easily sympathize, Madam Speaker, with the reasons why this remission order was given.
Looking at tariff remission orders published in the Gazette or Public Accounts, one can also find many examples where remissions are given because of anomalies in the Customs Tariff. For instance, a remission may be given of the duty on a piece of equipment not available in Canada, used to produce a product which can be imported duty free.
Finally, Madam Speaker, in any tax and tariff system, there are inevitably and regrettably administrative errors. Remission orders are also used to compensate the taxpayer or importer for such errors.
These procedures of remitting taxes and tariffs are an exceptional power, Madam Speaker, and the House might like to be assured that they are used only after careful consideration. I can supply that assurance.
In cases involving administration of the tax system, an internal Committee within Revenue Canada considers requests for remission. Further, tariff remissions are recommended only after detailed examination by an interdepartmental Committee and thorough consultations with parties who might be affected.
There are further steps in the approval process. The larger industrial tariff remission programs are always submitted to Cabinet. All tax remission orders now have to be approved by Treasury Board. Finally, all remission orders are examined by the Special Committee of the Council.

July 4, 1988
Financial Administration Act
Many of the cases I have mentioned constitute the only available remedy to rectify unfairness after the fact. There is another important function of remission orders, however, and that is to provide timely relief where a problem is ongoing or continuous.
As Members will recognize, our legislative calendar is crowded and it is a time-consuming process to change legislation. In these circumstances, remission orders may be used until a problem can be corrected by legislation.
A case in point is the "beer cooler" order passed on March 30, 1988. This order originated because a brewer wanted to get into the "hot" cooler market with a product blending both wine and beer. The problem was that excise tax is paid on wine used to produce the blend and another excise tax would apply to the finished product. To avoid double taxation, a remission order was issued. Should there be a continuing demand for this product, no doubt there will be a change proposed in the relevant tax legislation. What the remission order demonstrates, Madam Speaker, is the willingness of the government to act fast to remove roadblocks that would otherwise get in the way of the private sector going about their business.
Of course, Madam Speaker, there is a possible conflict between the levels of approval required in careful use of this exceptional policy instrument and its function of providing timely relief. Indeed, the Auditor-General has complained about the time taken to pass some remission orders. This is one of the reasons why Treasury Board is being removed from the remission approval process. This has already occurred in the case of tariffs and is also being considered for tax remission orders.
Action is also being undertaken to replace other longstanding remission orders by statutory provision. A case in point is the duties that have to be paid on goods admitted for temporary use in Canada.
Present practice is to remit all but a specified fraction of the full duty on these products and to record this as a remission. When these temporary entries are covered by regulation in the near future, over $200 million will disappear from the value of remission orders recorded in the Public Accounts.
Madam Speaker, that is my position concerning the motion sponsored by my colleague, and I should think it faithfully reflects the Government position in this debate.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL OF SECTION 17
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak for a few minutes on this particular motion. This motion attempts to increase the accountability of the Government of Canada to the Parliament of Canada and, consequently, to the people of Canada.
The Member for York East (Mr. Redway), and in fact all of his colleagues on the Public Accounts Committee, believe very strongly that there is a real need to increase the accountability of the Government in ways which make it possible to zero in
on expenditures which can be looked at. In doing so we found that there are a lot of tax expenditures made by the Government by very simple strokes of the pen which no one can really get their hands on. Not only are we concerned that this can be done easily, there is no mechanism to require Parliament to pass such expenditures.
Government Departments must include their expenditures within the Estimates that are passed by Parliament. However, Government expenditures in the form of tax remissions or credits do not have to pass through Parliament. Consequently, one could almost call these illegal expenditures because a fundamental principle is that such expenditures must be approved by the Parliament of Canada.
According to Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act, the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he considers it is in the public interest, may remit any tax, fee or penalty. In theory, this may be money being paid to the Government which it is turning back, perhaps for a good reason. However, parliamentary democracy requires that those types of expenditures, even indirect expenditures, should be made by the Parliament of Canada. That is not the case with remission orders, and that is why I support the motion of the Hon. Member for York East which suggests that Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act be repealed and that all remissions of taxes, fees or penalties be submitted each year to Parliament for approval.
While this may sound like a long and involved process, it would not take long to pass it through the House and would require Members to consider what happens in the remission process. For example, the Public Accounts of Canada, Volume II, contains many pages of remission orders which have never been passed by Parliament. They have only been registered as expenditures that have taken place.
The repeal of Section 17 and the addition of a requirement for parliamentary approval would establish control over a considerable amount of money. The latest Public Accounts of Canada, fiscal year 1986-87, contains 36 pages of remission orders totalling over $1 billion. Certain remission orders amounted to over $1 million in themselves, so we are not only concerned with small amounts of money.
A principle of democracy is that everyone be treated the same. This section of the Financial Administration Act allows Cabinet to return tax to anyone at any time for any reason. This leaves room for inequality when Parliament can only consider the Public Accounts reports that are filed perhaps a year after the expenditures have been made or moneys theoretically returned.
There are many good reasons for these remission orders and in most cases Parliament would approve them without difficulty. The point is that they would be considered by Parliament.
July 4, 1988

The tax credit is not covered by this Act, but the principle is the same. The previous Liberal Government provided for a research tax credit which companies that applied could use for a reduction in taxes. The tax credit cost us some $3.4 billion. We might have saved a considerable amount of that if the research tax credit were open to parliamentary scrutiny so that the list of applicants and the credits would have to be approved before the reduction in taxes were allowed. That is the type of procedure that has been suggested in this motion.
We need to review the process of tax expenditure to make sure that all tax money that is spent or credits that are given are authorized by the Parliament of Canada. It has been suggested that 30 per cent more in funds would go to Government coffers with the elimination of all tax expenditures and remission orders. I know that will not happen, but the point is that the remission of tax orders and the tax credit structure accounts for a very substantial part of expenditure. We must examine how to improve the whole structure.
The Public Accounts Committee has dealt with a number of remission orders. One of them is the Hudson's Bay Oil and Gas Company Limited, which cost us $400 million. It is that kind of operation which Parliament should be able to scrutinize before it takes place.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first, I want to express my congratulations to the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) for introducing this particular motion. It is very important that Canadians understand as much about this process as they possibly can since it is so important to us all.
I welcome the opportunity to make a few comments on tariff remission under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act and the new tariff remission authority, Section 101 of the Customs Tariff.
The last time this motion was debated, two of the speakers talked about the openness and accountability of the remission process. Earlier today, we heard about fairness and equity in the process. I would like at this time to speak in greater detail about the tariff remission process itself. I believe that this is important because, as noted during the last debate by my colleague, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Vincent), there is in fact a rather low level of public understanding of the workings of the tax and tariff remission system.
Prior to January 1, 1988, tariff remissions were introduced pursuant to Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. However, with the introduction of the new Customs Tariff on that date, most tariff remissions are now made pursuant to Section 101 of the Customs Tariff. As such, most remissions of customs duties would be outside the scope of the motion currently before the House. However, there will no doubt be occasions where certain remissions may still be introduced
Financial Administration Act
under Section 17, notably those affecting imports made prior to January 1, 1988.
While the wording of the tariff remission authorities allows a very broad use without any real restriction, in fact, the vast majority of duty remissions are introduced primarily as remedies in specific cases where the application of the tariff laws and regulations would lead to anomalous, inequitable, or unreasonable results or hardship. The Order in Council remission authorities allow for a quick response by the Government in these very disturbing cases. On March 31, 1988, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) introduced the first report to Parliament on remission orders.
I would like to point out some cases that were sometimes anomalous, inequitable, unreasonable and caused hardship. In this respect I would like to list just a few of the remissions that have been granted, as well as the dollar amounts involved. In
1987,	the remission of a customs duty and a portion of the sales tax paid or payable on stoves and ovens imported into Canada by Riverside Lions Non-Profit Housing of Winnipeg, which is in my riding, amounted to $9,940. This was done to assist this group in its efforts to furnish apartments for the disabled with stoves and ovens with special features designed to meet the needs of handicapped persons. That was a very important use of a remission order.
Again, in 1987, on the basis of extreme hardship, the amount remitted for a refund that would have been payable to the taxpayer had she fded on time was $654.
Further, in 1988, to prevent financial hardship to a gentleman, particularly in recognition of the fact that the repairs made to his vehicle were covered by warranty with a company in the United States, some $2,676 was remitted.
Again, in 1988, an order remitted on the grounds of administrative error concerning a 1982 tax and interest charge relating to a statute-barred claim for partial dependency of a physically infirm brother was $212.
Again, in 1988, a remission order conditionally remitted on the grounds of an administrative error statute-barred income tax for 1981 and 1982 on registered pension plan contributions which could not benefit from a tax free roll-over to an RRSP was $3,258. The condition was that the funds minus the pension deduction must be transferred to an RRSP before
1988.
We can see that these remission orders are very often granted to rectify cases of extreme hardship to individuals and to groups doing good things in our society.
The primary responsibility for these tariff remissions rests with the Department of Finance. Tariff remissions introduced for administrative reasons are sponsored by Revenue Canada.
The role of the Treasury Board with respect to the remission process under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act has been to provide a central ministerial forum in which to discuss and debate proposed remissions, in particular the most

July 4, 1988
Financial Administration Act
contentious ones. The board makes recommendations on remission proposals to a special committee of Council, which in turn makes the final recommendation to the Governor-General in Council. The remission process usually starts with a representation to the Government. Most of these are received from importers or Canadian manufacturers who believe that, for one reason or another, they should be granted tariff relief on particular products that they are importing. It is very important on an ongoing basis that there be extensive consultation carried out with all the parties who might be affected by this remission.
The Government of Canada has made several improvements to the duty remission process. First, there is a new regulatory process which requires that a regulatory impact analysis statement be prepared for all tariff remissions, and that the statement be published in the Canada Gazette along with remission orders. Once the remission order has been approved by the Governor in Council, it is published in the Canada Gazette. This is another recent improvement in the process since, in the past, not all orders were gazetted.
Furthermore, all orders remitting over $20 million in duties are tabled in the House shortly after being approved. It is very clear that a $20 million level is set at one place while my colleague, the Hon. Member for York East, would want it to be much lower than that. In another Private Bill to be discussed by the House, Bill C-287, a suggestion is being made that orders over $1 million be tabled in this House before being approved. I think all of us want to recognize that remission orders are very important to the people to whom they are granted. I would not quibble if the $20 million level were set down considerably lower than that.
If the foregoing were not enough to make the remission process open and accountable, the Minister of Finance has undertaken to table in the House, twice a year, a report on all new remissions giving information on their costs and the reasons why they were introduced.
It is rather obvious from this report to Parliament on remission orders that these are done by and large for needy and worth-while cases in small dollar amounts. None of us would want to discontinue the process of granting small dollar remissions for very important causes to individual Canadians. What is at stake here is the accountability of Parliament and the fairness of these decisions.
In closing, 1 will say that the Government of Canada and the Minister of Finance have introduced several changes which make the system more accountable and more fair. None of us would quibble with any suggestions that Hon. Members would make to make the system even fairer and more accountable. I offer the following comment. If we were to introduce every single remission order for adoption in Parliament, then very important cases, very needy cases, might be unnecessarily delayed in a bureaucratic fashion.
I wish to commend the Hon. Member for York East on his suggestion that remission orders be made more accountable to
the House of Commons, but would suggest that having every single one of them heard here might in fact hurt those people who the Hon. Member is trying to support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in this debate and say a few things about the motion that is before us. It is a motion standing in the name of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of repealing Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act and require that all remissions of taxes, fees or penalties be submitted, each year, to Parliament for approval.
Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act states that the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he considers it in the public interest, may remit any tax, fee or penalty. Remission orders are somewhat different from tax expenditures. Parliament has to vote on tax expenditures. In remission orders there is no scrutiny by Parliament, or accountability by the Cabinet to Parliament. It is totally a decision by Cabinet on recommendations from the Treasury Board. That is how remission orders work.
While we support the thrust of the motion of the Hon. Member for York East, it seems to me that there is something more to it than just giving the information to The Gazette, and it is more than having the information. That is only a small part of it. In this review process I do not think that all remission orders need to be looked at. One has to realize that some are for very small amounts and time should not be spent reviewing all of them. I agree with the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Boyer) that tax remissions of $1 million and up ought to be reviewed.
However, there is more to it than that. We need to know the rationale behind the tax remission. Why was it given? What was the reason for the tax remission? Why was this money turned back to the taxpayer corporation or individual? There must be a statement of explanation from the applicant for the tax remission.
I recognize that many are justifiable. For example, investors in the Principal Group were being taxed on interest that they had not received. It is only fair that a remission order should be put in abeyance to collect that tax, because the investors had not collected the interest from their investment in the Principal Group. That makes sense.
There is one example that I have had difficulty with, and my colleague, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore, has raised it in the House. I wish to give him credit for that. One has to keep in mind that it is a Conservative Government and these ideas are coming from Conservative back-benchers. It is important that we keep the focus. The Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore has raised the question about Goodyear Tire Inc. in his riding. That company has received $63 million
July 4, 1988

in tax and duty remissions. It has a bit of a fight going on with the union in the shop. It wants to get rid of the union. There are provisions for that type of thing within the Labour Act. Lo and behold, Goodyear has decided to close down its operation in the riding of Etobicoke-Lakeshore and move down the road to Napanee. It has received $63 million in tax and duty remissions. Then the Peterson Liberal Government of Ontario runs in and says: "Here, you will need some money to start a plant in Napanee, so we'll give you $32 million". Out of the public largesse, the Ontario Government has given Goodyear $32 million to locate in Napanee.
As one studies this particular case one finds out that Goodyear's headquarters in Akron, Ohio, has readjusted its administrative charge structure to the branch plant at Etobicoke-Lakeshore and it will receive the bulk of that $63 million. The bulk of that $63 million will be siphoned off in a pipeline to Akron, Ohio, from the Treasury of Ottawa, and zipped off to the parent company in Akron, Ohio. Members of Parliament have not and will not have an opportunity to review that situation.
When Goodyear does not pay that $63 million, someone else has to pay it. When companies such as Goodyear do not pay their share of taxes, the ordinary Canadian out there has to pick up the shortfall. I do not believe that in a democracy where that type of remission is being given it ought to go unexamined by those who are elected to Parliament to do that job.
While we support the general thrust of the motion of the Hon. Member for York East, we do believe that not only should there be a review, but there should be a statement of explanation accompanying each of those remission orders. As I stated previously, we do not need to look at all remission orders, but a good starting point would be anything from a million dollars up.
If we can approve this particular motion, it does not necessarily mean that the system will be changed tomorrow. I hope that anyone who is watching or listening understands that. This is simply a motion that suggests to the Government that this is what ought to be done. It is a suggestion that is coming from a Conservative back-bencher, and it is supported by other Progressive Conservatives. I know it is a contradiction in terms to think that there is such a thing as a Progressive Conservative, but there is the odd one. I want to make the plea that there is an odd closet Progressive Conservative sitting on the back-benches, or on the front benches. The Government would do well to listen to those voices of reason. From time to time they do have the odd reasonable suggestion, and this is one for which the Government would find support from the NDP side of the House. I do not know where the Liberals stand on it, but the NDP would certainly support a move to give this type of accountability to the whole question of tax and duty remissions.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBER'S BUSINESS-MOTIONS   FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION ACT SUGGESTED REPEAL OF SECTION 17
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) made a speech in
Financial Administration Act
February, 1984, to the Young Presidents' Organization, at which time he called for changes in the administration of the Government of Canada, opening up the process to greater public scrutiny, and particularly a more important role for elected representatives in the decision-making process. I believe that that was very firmly part of the mandate for change that came later in that year of 1984.
If that is the general proposition, it has to come to rest in particular terms. No better example could be found than in the practice of the Government in granting remission orders under Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act. This practice developed over some time. Previous Governments were counselled to use Section 17 in an ever-expanding interpretation. The Hon. Member for St. Boniface (Mr. Duguay) who spoke a few moments ago correctly stated that the purpose of Section 17 was to correct the anomalies, the patent injustices, and the unusual workings of the Income Tax Act.
What we have seen happen, in addition to that, has been the practice for Governments to use remission orders as a means for implementing industrial policy. No one would say that Governments should not have an industrial policy. But the point here is that an industrial policy should not be carried out in a hip-pocket or off-the-record fashion, which Orders in Council granting remission orders are, but rather here on the floor of the House of Commons where Members on all sides who are informed on these issues would have an opportunity to debate, approve, or oppose.
This is not something that has been a concern only for Members of Parliament. In the 1979 decision of Clarkson Co. Ltd. v. The Queen (1979) 94 D.L.R. (3d) 348, 365, the Chief Justice of the Federal Court of Appeal queried whether Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act was meant to authorize general remission orders which effectively amend the relevant taxing statute, as opposed to the remission of specific tax liability in individual cases.
To me, as a lawyer, that is an extraordinary development when you have a judge opining in the process of a decision that here is a section of the law being used not for its intended purpose but in fact to amend legislation and to do it outside of this Chamber, which is the place where law is passed.
Parliamentarians have focused on this in other forms as well, most certainly the Standing Committee on Public Accounts. The New Democrat Member from Saskatchewan earlier referred to such celebrated cases as the Hudson's Bay oil and gas remission order in 1986, as being worth some $4.5 million, but the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, in its Issue No. 26 of its report to this House, estimated the value of that remission order being in fact in excess of $1 billion.
So we are not dealing here with the small amounts that are forgiven from time to time because of unjust workings of the Income Tax Act. We are dealing with the practice that has

July 4, 1988
Financial Administration Act
developed for Governments to use remission orders as a means of implementing industrial policy.
My view is that we have a trend under way now in the House to come to grips with this problem. Certainly, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), on March 6 of 1987, when he responded to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts by letter, saying that he would henceforth table in the House remission orders exceeding $20 million in value, along with an explanation of those remission orders twice yearly, made a step further than what he was strictly required to do. We have the resolution of the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) on the floor today, where he goes all the way, and I understand completely his motivation for this, because he shares the concern which I voiced in this Chamber many times that we have witnessed the use of remission orders but we have also, most assuredly, witnessed the abuse of remission orders. His motion before us is an effort to correct that.
Being a moderate, as I am, perhaps there is a compromise position between the stage to which the Finance Minister has moved to date, namely, $20 million and twice-annual summaries tabled in the House, and the position of the Hon. Member for York East, which is saying that every single remission order, even if it is for $11.14, should come before Parliament.
In the Bill which I have introduced on March 16th of this year, Bill C-287, I am proposing a $1 million threshold, and two further features. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) has already referred to this Bill, but there are two further features in it. One is that the remission order be accompanied by a justification report. It would be in this way that the Minister of Finance would explain to Members of the House of Commons what justifies giving such an order, along the lines of what we used to see under the Foreign Investment Review Act when justification had to be given that there was net benefit to Canada for this investment to be made. What is the net benefit to Canada of $63 million being granted, for example, to Goodyear Canada Inc.? What benefits outweigh that cost? These should be specified in a justification report, as I am proposing in my Bill.
Second, I am saying that there should be a 60-day period for those remission orders in the House during which the House can approve them or reject them and, at the end of the 60-day period, because the Government must get on and function, if nothing has been done at the end of 60 days, then those remission orders would take effect, without Parliament having voiced an opinion, yea or nay, on the particular remission orders.
As it stands, we now have the Minister of Finance bringing in his report to Parliament on remission orders. This has already been alluded to by previous speakers. I would like to say why I think this is an inadequate step along the direction that we must be going, although it is a step in the right direction, most assuredly.
The reason I say that-and I am contrasting it to what would be included in the justification report-is that here, for example, if one picks one of the remission orders that I am quite familiar with, that given to Goodyear, one finds that the first column is a description of the order; the second column is a sponsoring department or agency; the third column cites the applicable legislation; the fourth column shows the total amount for the life of the order; and the final, fifth column, gives the reasons for the order. Here is where we begin to come face to face with reality. The reason for this one was, to Goodyear, to facilitate the modernization and rationalization of tire production facilities "in order to prevent further plant closures and thus maintain current production and employment levels".
I am not going to take the few moments available to me now to repeat what I said earlier on the floor of the House, but let me say it in brief compass as follows. Those familiar with the two tire manufacturing plants which Goodyear has in Canada in Valleyfield, Quebec, and Medicine Hat in Alberta, understand well that there is no amount of government assistance that will make any difference to the level of production or the number of jobs at either of those plants, for reasons of market forces and tied selling to the GM plant at Ste Therese, Quebec, which last year the Government supported with $210 billion of additional funding. So that production and those jobs are secure.
Then it goes on and says, "to maintain current employment levels". We know in fact that the closure of one plant and the loss of 1,574 jobs in Etobicoke-Lakeshore is matched by the new plant with its projected employment of 800 new jobs. So that in fact is a net loss. This statement in the Minister's report to the House about justifying this report on the basis of maintaining current employment levels does not accurately state what the reality is. It is for that reason that I believe, fundamentally, we should have the opportunity on the floor of the House to hear the contentions made in defence of remission orders, and the opportunity to bring other facts that contradict those on the floor for debate and discussion.
In fact, I would conclude with these two observations. I do not think that any of these efforts, to permit the use of Section 17 or other measures like this, for industrial policy, is the right way to go. Leave remission orders for what they were intended to be, to clear up the anomalous results that are occasionally found-the unfair consequences of the workings of the law. If the Government of the day, of any stripe, feels that it is important to support the Canadian tire industry, then let it bring, on the floor of the House of Commons, a statute called, shall we say, the Canadian Tire Manufacturers Assistance Act, 1988. There we can deal not only with Goodyear, but with Uniroyal and with Michelin, because they both received remission orders as well. We can debate as parliamentarians whether the $100 million or the $200 million that will be the benefit for those companies is worth it. If it is not possible to have that kind of legislation brought before Parliament under the framework of our new trade treaty with the United States

This issue has not for the first time come before the courts. I have already referred to a 1979 decision. Madam Speaker, the motion before us has been put by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway). I know him well and I know his continuing interest in matters, especially those arising out of the Public Accounts Committee on which he has served and for which he has become somewhat well known. The motion states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of repealing Section 17 of the Financial Administration Act and require that all remissions of taxes, fees or penalties be submitted, each year, to Parliament for approval.
I do not have any real difficulty with the general intent of the motion, which is to bring greater accountability to the issuance of remission orders. I question whether or not the motion is sufficiently clear in that it does not really indicate what kind of approval would be sought from Parliament, whether it would be sought for every single remission order or whether it would be sought for matter in advance so that an order could not be granted without parliamentary approval.
Remission orders are used, I believe, because of time constraints sometimes imposed by the House to deal with matters like this in another way. For example, we could pass a Bill if we so chose. But I do not think anyone would suggest that Parliament should pass a Bill to grant a remission order for $654 to remit, on the basis of extreme hardship, the amount of the refund that would have been repayable to the taxpayer had he or she filed on time. Obviously I do not think that this is the intent of the motion, but that has not been made clear.
I suggest that what perhaps we could adopt is a practice whereby enshrined in law could be the tabling of a document by the Minister either annually or semi-annually, which could
Financial Administration Act
then be automatically referred to one of the standing committees of Parliament.
We have seen through parliamentary reform that all Governor in Council appointments are now referred to an appropriate standing committee. Speaking from the point of view of the committee with which I am most familiar, namely, the Finance Committee, we resolved that all appointments would be circulated to every member of the committee, and should any member of the committee, Government, Opposition or independent Member wish to have a witness called before the committee, he or she could notify the clerk, and the witness would then be called at an appropriate time. There is, however, very little use of the practice. We called the new Governor of the Bank of Canada earlier this year, but beyond that the practice has not been widely used. The practice has not been followed by other committees either, but that is not to say the practice is not working. What it has done by allowing automatic review of government appointments by a standing committee is to put upon the Government a greater onus to act with a little extra care and to be more conscious of who is appointed to boards, agencies and committees of government because these appointments may be subject to parliamentary scrutiny.
1 suggest the same principle could be applied here and that having now received this first report from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), who has committed himself to table such a report annually in Parliament, we could enshrine that practice. The current Minister has said he will do that, and I have no doubt he will, but future Ministers may not necessarily continue the practice. If we were to enshrine the need to table such a report semi-annually or annually in Parliament allowing it then to be deemed referred to an appropriate standing committee, the committee would then have the authority to review any or all of the remissions that have been granted. Again, as has been the case with Governor in Council appointments, I suggest that that possibility of scrutiny alone would serve to cause the Government to act with a great deal of care in the granting of such remission orders.
I myself have sought to have a remission order granted for a constituent of mine, so I can understand why the practice needs to be in place. It would allow the Government to act in cases where inequities, anomalies or other things occur that were never contemplated when the Act was passed. As yet I have not been successful but I can describe the case briefly.
A constituent of mine inherited a piece of property from a relative who had passed away. At the time of the death, property values were very high.
