I welcome this opportunity, Madam Speaker, to speak in this important debate on the proposed legislation implementing the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. Madam Speaker, although we just voted on a motion for time allocation, I think we should ask ourselves why the Government decided to limit debate in this way. Today's discussion is one of the most important ones we have had in this House for some time, and we should ask ourselves what the Government has in mind. Why does it want to limit debate? One of the first answers that comes to mind is that perhaps the Government is afraid Canadians will find out too much about this free trade agreement.
Recent polls have shown that public opinion is starting to change. People are no longer convinced that this agreement is such a good thing for Canada. Maybe that is why the Governmment wants to push this legislation through the House. We are told, Madam Speaker, that since the Second World War, customs duty dropped from an average of 20 per cent to an average of 9 per cent. We also know that 80 per cent of our trade with the United States is duty free, and that the average duty on the remaining 20 per cent is 9 per cent. So why is the Government rushing to sign an agreement for which it received no mandate? In fact, when he was Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said it would be unwise for Canada to sign an agreement with the United States. He used the metaphor of the mouse that gets in bed with an elephant. It could be a crushing experience!
July 4, 1988

Today we heard we shouldn't be afraid of the Americans. We should get together and trade and do business with them. Of course we shouldn't be afraid of the Americans. I believe that we as Canadians have enough maturity to take care of ourselves, without clinging to the coattails of the Americans. We shouldn't be afraid of the Americans, but, Madam Speaker, we should not get so close that our identity might be threatened. And I am afraid that this agreement could be a definite threat to our Canadian identity. There lies the danger.
Today we heard Hon. Members comparing the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement to the European Common Market. I don't think we can draw a parallel between the two. It's like comparing apples and oranges. We have a population of 25 million in Canada, while the Americans have ten times that: 250 million. It is indeed an opportunity to be run over and swallowed up. That is where the parallel ends; there is no possible comparison with the European Common Market.
When this agreement was discussed, Canadians were assured that there was no question of signing it unless some concessions were obtained from the Americans. First was guaranteed access to the U.S. market of 250 million consumers. We were also promised, we were told that there would be a commission to settle trade disputes between the two countries. People are trying to have us believe that the agreement gives us guaranteed access to the American market. But I cannot find this guarantee anywhere in the agreement. Access to the U.S. market will only be guaranteed if Canadians produce high quality goods at competitive prices. That is what gives us guaranteed access; the agreement will not be able to do that.
We could talk for a long time about the binational commission. It exists, it is there in the agreement. But unfortunately, this commission has no power except to see whether the countervailing measures sought comply with the law of the country concerned. If so, the commission can do absolutely nothing about it! We are not exempt from duties imposed by American laws.
During the debate, we also said that the Province of New Brunswick supported this free trade agreement. I will point out to you, Madam Speaker, that the Premier of New Brunswick, Mr. McKenna, nevertheless set some conditions, which have not yet been met.
One condition set was to ensure that regional development programs are not subject to countervailing duties. This condition has not yet been met.
A second condition is that Canada no longer be subject to protectionist measures. The omnibus bill is still alive and has not been dealt with. So, Madam Speaker, this condition has not been met.
We had also asked for an adjustment program for our food processing sector. This condition has not yet been met. We in New Brunswick have reason to be concerned for this food processing industry.

Madam Speaker, I would like to begin by emphasizing that in his book Where I stand, published in 1983, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney),

July 4, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
who was already Party Leader then, puts forward his position on all of the main questions, the major issues the country faced in 1983, five years ago, and there is no mention whatsoever of free trade as the key policy of a Government he would be heading.
I would like to make a few comments on free trade because I believe that Canadian men and women should remind the Conservative Government that it has no mandate to sign the free trade agreement that is now before the House of Commons. In fact, in 1983, the Prime Minister did not claim to be for, but rather against a free trade agreement with the United States, and he stated that the issue had been settled in 1911 under Prime Minister Wilfrid Laurier, and settled for good, as far as he was concerned. It was not an issue to be settled in the future. Indeed, it was not an issue at all. Until he became Prime Minister. Just one year after his election, in 1984, he suddenly presented Canadian men and women with a free trade policy, by beginning negotiations with the United States on a bilateral free trade agreement, with no mandate whatsoever from Canadians for the negotiation of such an accord.
Indeed, Madam Speaker, the Government has totally bypassed the process it should have followed, according to me, my Party, and the vast majority of Canadians, which is that before launching negotiations with the United States, it should have obtained a mandate for a decision that is so fundamental to the future of our country.
Madam Speaker, we have now five days of debate on second reading of Bill C-130. The Government has given us no assurance that the committee will have adequate time to consider these matters. The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) gives us no such assurance and may in fact be considering the possibility that the Bill be sent back to the House within five or ten days.
It is all very well, Madam Speaker, that the committees subscribed fully to the principle of free trade, but they never had access to the agreement itself. Even the committee that sat in the fall, Madam Speaker, had no choice but to draft its final report without access to the agreement, since it was still being drafted in Washington by the Americans and the Canadians.
These past few months, whenever I met with my constituents as well as other Canadian men and women both in Quebec and elsewhere, I asked them: Do you want to have an election before Canada gets involved once and for all with the United States through this free trade agreement? Eighty per cent of them said yes. Madam Speaker, such is also the case of the most recent polls which indicate that the small majority who favoured the free trade agreement are now a minority. Now, most Canadian men and women who have an opinion on this issue are against it. It should also be emphasized that the feeling among those who are opposed to the free trade agreement is a lot stronger than among those who support it.
The men and women who support the Free Trade Agreement come mainly from the business world. It is the Business Council on National Issues, a club made up of the chairmen
and chief executive officers of all the main Canadian and multinational corporations in Canada, which is behind the Government. When business people tell this Tory Government to do something, the Tories say: Yes sir, we will go ahead. And that is what they are doing, Madam Speaker. They went directly to the United States to fill the order of the business people for a free trade agreement. Did they do so because it would benefit the ordinary people of Chicoutimi, the Gaspe, British Columbia or even Lac-Saint-Jean? The answer is no.
For instance, Madam Speaker, I personally visited Lac-Saint-Jean during the by-election campaign. I realized that the economic situation in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area has not changed a bit over the past four years under a Tory government. No regional development program has been implemented. No effort has been made by the Government to remedy the unemployment situation which exceeded 13 per cent when I was there! Madam Speaker, the reduction was maybe 1 or 2 per cent. Since 1984, in that area, the unemployment rate has been higher since the Tory Party came to power than it had been during the recession, say, between 1980 and 1982 under the previous government.
Now, because of the by-election, the Government was compelled to set up a regional development program, but without this program, would the promises made by the present Secretary of State (Mr. Bouchard) have been formulated? The answer is clearly no.
Will the free trade agreement really benefit those people? I don't think so for the following reasons. First of all, since most of the industrial jobs which will be created, if such jobs are created, will be based along the Montreal-Windsor corridor, the rest of the regions, including Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean, will not be affected.
Secondly, we can see that the investments in this region are mostly basic investments, and resource investments, for which no tariff barriers exist between the U.S. and Canada. Thirdly, Madam Speaker, the same thing goes for the timber and lumber industry of that region. Has this industry ever been affected by pressures from the United States, by measures which will still be in effect five to seven years after the free trade deal, and which might never disappear?
The Americans still have the power to put pressure on us. In fact, they have forced Canada to levy a 15 per cent tax on softwood lumber exports, because they felt we were too competitive.
Finally, Madam Speaker, I have read in the newspapers that the governments of both Quebec and British Culumbia recently felt they had to send delegates not to Ottawa, but to Washington, to make sure that the U.S. royalties program relating to investments would allow Canadians to cancel the tax on softwood lumber exports from the provinces of Quebec and British Columbia.
July 4, 1988

And that, Madam Speaker, is the way we will have to handle things if this agreement is passed by our Parliament, by the U.S. Congress, and finally ratified before January 1.
Madam Speaker, I note for example that Quebec, under Clause 6 of the Bill, will have to adjust its legislation to the deal, or else we can expect that the Quebec legislation will be invalidated by the Canadian legislation, and even by the Canadian regulations and the Agreement.
Prime Minister Bourassa says that Quebec will adjust its legislation to the free trade deal. But let us suppose that our Governement is in power, that it is an NDP provincial Government or possibly a PQ Government, and that it does not accept a certain initiative taken by the Federal Governement. Will that Governement have the power to resist?
The answer is no since Quebec has handed over a great part of its powers to the Federal Government. That is what has been done by a Quebec Government, by a Liberal Governement in Quebec, Madam Speaker. And I believe that they are wrong in accepting this.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, according to Clause 8 of this bill, all Canadian legislation will be subordinated to the agreement as well as to Bill C-130 and the regulations pertaining thereto. That also is unacceptable.
Madam Speaker, my time has run out. I would like to speak a bit longer, but I believe that those in Quebec who think that they have made a great step forward with the free trade deal are wrong and that they will find that, unless they are able to stop this bill, in the final analysis Quebec will suffer a loss of freedom in terms of policy making and implementation. Having said that, Madam Speaker, I shall say no more, time forbidding.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the free trade agreement with the United States will do much to correct Canada's long existing regional economic disparities. It will do more than just give the entire country an economic boost; it will also help regions develop and gain strength, not only from their own regional markets but from the large and rich markets which stretch from coast to coast just south of our border.
Nowhere is the removal of impediments more important than in the international trading system. Everyone is hurt by protectionism. No one can doubt the gains conferred on all countries by the great era of trade liberalization under the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade.
Canada is firmly committed to working for freer trading rules in the vital multilateral negotiations of the Uruguay Round. Our agreement with the United States should in no way be seen as an alternative to or inconsistent with our determination to seek further liberalization through the GATT. Canada's commitment to liberalizing the rules is
Canada-V.S. Free Trade Agreement
demonstrated by our free trade agreement with the U.S. The agreement can and will serve as a useful model for the multilateral negotiations, notably including its ground breaking provisions covering the important area of trade in services.
It comes down to a decision on whether Canadians should seek the opportunity and the challenge now presented of securing and enhancing a combined market of 270 million or whether Canadians are prepared to face the real risk of restricted access to a market so vital to their prosperity.
Free trade will encourage job creating investment in energy projects across the country. As we well know, a greater supply means greater energy security for Canada in the future. In the northeast corner of Alberta we have the Athabasca oil sands. These oil sands have within them proven reserves greater than the reserves in Saudi Arabia, immense reserves available to Canada. We cannot bring those reserves on stream unless there is a certainty of demand.
One of the things that will flow from this agreement is that there will be certainty of demand which will guarantee Canada having "made-in-Canada, provided-in-Canada" energy from our own sources brought on-stream because of our arrangements. This is not a continental energy policy. Canada retains full control over all aspects of energy policy that relate to management of the resource base, transportation, or domestic use of energy resources.
What is true of petroleum and carbon resources in Alberta is also true of hydro resources in Ontario, Quebec, and elsewhere in our country. All these benefits will flow to Canada without compromising our ability to maintain agricultural marketing boards, regional development programs, our assistance to the cultural industry, or our wide array of social programs.
It has been argued that a free trade agreement with the United States would derogate from provincial jurisdiction. The free trade agreement does not in any way represent constitutional change or result in a constitutional amendment. It is an agreement between two sovereign nations and is subject to the provisions of the Constitution of Canada. Provincial responsibilities for such important matters as natural resources will be as full and complete after the agreement as they were before.
The free trade agreement provides an environment for the Canadian energy industries to secure and to expand their access to the United States. Our constitutional responsibility over our natural resources is not being eroded. Alberta will continue to own, to control, and to manage its resources on behalf of all Albertans.
I want to address four myths or misconceptions that I have heard being expounded during the current debate. The first is that the Canadian Government has been stampeded into this

July 4, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
agreement by paranoia about United States protectionism. In other words, it is alleged that the Government has miscalculated the seriousness of the protectionist threat in the United States and has placed unwarranted value on seeking secure access to the U.S. market. This analysis is false. The trend toward protectionism in the United States is long term and inexorable because it is driven by a fundamental change in the global balance of economic forces.
So long as the United States was the world's predominant economic power and enjoyed substantial technological advantage over its rivals, it was driven by self-interest and magnanimity alike to pursue a policy of liberal trade. The United States is still the world's largest, richest, and most dynamic market, and it is liable to remain so for the foreseeable future.
However, American economic and technological leadership has now been challenged on three successive fronts: First, by the resurgence of a revitalized Europe from the ashes of World World II; second, by the rise of an extraordinarily disciplined and dynamic Japan; and third, by the recent emergence of the newly industrialized countries, particularly on the Pacific Rim.
The second myth or misconception permeating the debate here is that the choice facing Canadians is between a familiar and relatively comfortable status quo and the unknown of free trade. There is no status quo. The world is always on the move. The only difference is that the world is moving far, far faster now than ever before. It is an illusion to talk about the status quo. It just does not exist.
Global technological and economic developments mean that Canada's resource base can no longer finance the maintenance of an inefficient manufacturing economy sheltering behind high tariff walls.
Even Canadian manufacturers have realized that they can no longer prosper from the domestic market alone. They need secure and free access to a larger market, especially the United States market, to invest and thus achieve economies of scale and specialization.
The third myth or misconception in Canada is that the multilateral trade negotiations under the GATT and bilateral trade deals with the United States possibly represent alternatives, indeed incompatible alternatives. Nothing could be further from the truth.
Regional free trade areas such as the European Community and the Canada-U.S. agreement are fully sanctioned under Article 24 of the GATT.
It would be foolhardy as Canadians to close our eyes to these developments and to rely exclusively on a multilateral trading system whose effectiveness is unfortunately eroding and whose undertakings and disciplines are too generalized, too vague, and too narrow in scope to provide an effective brake to U.S. protectionism.
The fourth myth about the agreement is that it will result in a loss of Canadian sovereignty or independence. If by independence we are talking about the right of Canadians to maintain the unique set of social support measures such as medicare, unemployment insurance, and the Canada Pension Plan, nothing in the agreement prevents Canadian Governments from maintaining these programs.
There is no way that the federal Government would trash medicare, old age pensions, unemployment insurance, or other important social programs. Any politician who tried that would not make history, but would be history.
If free trade results in a loss of sovereignty, let us ask our New Zealand friends how they are making out with the Australians, or the Austrians or the Swedes, whether they have been taken over by other members of the European trade agreement.
Even in the European Community where a measure of political integration has been consciously undertaken, no one ever hears the Danes or the Dutch complain that their culture is being Teutonized or Anglocized as a result of a common commercial market.
One third of Canada's Gross National Product comes from exports. Close to three million Canadian jobs are directly related to exports, and 78 per cent to 80 per cent of our exports go to the United States. Canada must secure the high level of trade we have with the United States. We must bring in a dispute resolution mechanism that is contained in the free trade agreement, and we must enhance U.S. trade to create jobs and maintain our standard of living.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose I hit a bit of a sore spot there. It was the same speech on the same topic.
Today and tomorrow, many Members of Parliament of all three Parties will be sharing their views on the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. My Government and my Party have proposed this historic agreement, and I want to say that I am strongly in favour of it.
It is interesting that on some issues it is difficult for the public to see how the three Parties may differ. In the case of the free trade agreement, however, the picture is very clear. The Progressive Conservative Government is whole-heartedly
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
in favour of it and both opposition Parties are totally against it. The battle lines have been drawn. In the next election, Canadians from coast to coast will be able to tell us if they want a bigger, healthier Canada because of the free trade agreement.
The importance to Canada of the FTA cannot be exaggerated. Currently almost 80 per cent of our exports flow to the United States. These exports account for 25 per cent of everything we produce, and over two million jobs are dependent on trade. For over 100 years, most Canadian Governments have pursued improved trading relations with the United States. In the early 1850s, Canadian farmers and commercial interests wanted a trading agreement with the United States. Our economy had become vulnerable due to Britain's commitment toward free trade.
For over 80 years, Canada had imported more goods from the United States than it had from Great Britain. However, up until 1942, our exports to the U.S. were less than those to Great Britain. This changed in 1942. Since then, the United States has been our number one market for exports. As stated earlier, the Americans now buy almost 80 per cent of the goods and services we export.
There have been attempts in the past by Governments to diminish our dependency on the U.S. by trying to increase trade with Britain and other European countries and with Pacific Rim countries. Their attempts to implement this strategy were not successful. Indeed, our trade with the United States increased during this period.
Professor David J. Bercuson of the University of Calgary sums up the situation very well with these remarks:
Much has changed in Canada since the reciprocity treaty of 1854, the 1911 General Election, or the uncertain days of the late 1940's.
Now it is the manufacturers who most want free trade while the farmers are reticent.
Now it is the Liberals who oppose free trade, even though the Liberal Party has traditionally been its major supporter.
But one overall factor remains as it did in 1948, in 1911 and earlier: There are those Canadians confident of the future and of their identity as Canadians, who seek to expand trade across the globe but who also want to compete as equals in the U.S. market.
And there are still those who, out of fear, wave the flag and shout jeremiads about the future of a Canada linked to free trade and the United States.
They are certain as their forebears were, that Canada is a fragile country that will not be able to resist the siren call of total immersion with the great republic.
Times and faces have changed, but the message remains the same.
I agree that times and faces have changed. I do not believe that Canadians will be swayed by emotional, flag waving scare tactics. Canadians know the world is changing. They realize that no country can be an economic island when an integrated global economy is emerging. The private sector in Canada had a brutal reminder of this during the recession of the early 1980s.

July 4, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
It is abundantly clear that our service, production, and distribution sectors are affected by competitive companies in other countries around the globe. Canadians do not seem to be aware of how strongly the business community in Canada supports the free trade agreement. For over 100 years, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association supported tariffs with the United States. In 1983, however, it made a dramatic reversal by appearing before the Macdonald Commission in support of a bilateral trade agreement with the United States.
Many other businesses also submitted briefs in support of the FTA. Surely if the small business community, which generates most of the jobs and wealth in Canada, believes the FTA will mean economic benefits to Canada, then Canadians should not be seduced by the emotional arguments of the doomsayers, the Liberals and the NDP. Liberal and NDP Members say that the Tories want to hand over our jobs and our future. This is nonsense.
The energy sector is another area where the Opposition has tried to mislead Canadians into believing we will surrender control over energy. This assertion is false and opposition Members know it. Canada will still be able to control the pace of development and production of its energy resources. Canada will still be able to prohibit foreign takeovers of financially healthy oil and gas companies. Canada will continue to be able to use fiscal incentives to encourage exploration and development. Canada will retain its right to cushion the impact of any future sharp energy price increases by regulating prices or using the national tax transfer systems. Obviously, we are not losing control of our energy resources.
Many myths about the loss of our sovereignty and our culture are being propagated by the Liberals and the NDP. Again, the facts refute these myths. During the last two years of negotiations, opposition Parties have gloomily predicted that the Canadian Government would be pressured to give up important and highly regarded social policies such as unemployment insurance and free medical care. However, none of our social policies have been bargained away, not one.
The FTA protects current policies in two ways. The grandfathering principle has been applied to almost all things other than trade in goods, even if they are inconsistent with the rule of national treatment. This is applicable to a wide range of policies such as those prohibiting the sale of viable Canadian oil firms to foreign interests, to those regulating the export of raw logs.
In addition, many sensitive industries are totally exempted from any national treatment obligation. These include all cultural industries, day care, health, education, and Crown corporations.
Another falsehood being touted by the Opposition is that somehow the free trade agreement will be detrimental to women. In fact, free trade will deliver enhanced benefits to Canadian women as workers and as consumers. Many of the new jobs to be created will be in the service industries where female employment is already dominant.
High tariff barriers are particularly harmful to women since a larger proportion of their pay goes toward the purchase of basic necessities such as food, clothing, and living accommodations which are more expensive because of tariffs. Women can be winners from the free trade agreement. They have the innate capacity to adjust to changes in the workplace and the market-place.
I have talked to many men, women, and young people from Markham and Whitchurch-Stouffville about the free trade agreement. Some have genuine concerns, some lack enough information, and many are being influenced by the fear tactics of the opposition Parties and the media. However, on balance, I believe most residents of the area of Markham are supportive and they know that today's youth will benefit in the future through job creation opportunities.
I would like to end with the words of Professor John Crispo who said:
It will be a shame and tragedy if the proponents of the Free Trade
Agreement allow its detractors to so dishonestly distort its significance for the
country's long-run well-being that the F.T.A. somehow goes down to defeat.
Mr. Macdonald who headed the commission believes so strongly that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) is wrong to denounce the free trade agreement that he will not campaign for the Liberals in the next federal election. It will be the first election in almost 35 years that he will miss. Another high profile, long time Liberal, Milton Harris of Harris Steel, has abandoned the Liberal Party for its irresponsible anti-free trade stance.
I believe that Canadians have all the necessary facts about the free trade agreement and, when all the emotional and fear mongering myths have been dispelled, they will embrace the initiative with enthusiasm. Canadians do not run from challenges. They certainly will not turn their backs on the greatest economic opportunity of the century. The free trade agreement is a nation building initiative if there ever was one. Let us get on with the job and get it passed by this House and the other place.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate this evening. Not only am I pleased, in fact I feel it is a duty to participate in this debate on free trade because it is such an important debate.
This debate is about our roots. I say that because when most of us trace our roots back a couple of generations we realize that our grandparents settled this country to establish trade centres here. If our ancestors were French, they probably penetrated the St. Lawrence area in the 1620s to establish trade centres to trade with their mother country. If our ancestors were British, they came in through the Hudson Bay area in the 1670s and again established trade centres. Those settlements competed with one another for the trade available in this country. Our ancestors grew up around trade. They came here because they saw an opportunity on this continent to better themselves and to provide a way of life for their families.
Cycles come and go. Trade moved to the West as settlers moved into Canada, and during a period after 1850 the Atlantic area had to push its trade west for a number of reasons. First, there was a civil war in the United States and Atlantic Canadians sensed that the United States was becoming increasingly hostile to its neighbours to the North. Second, the British stopped giving Canada preferential treatment as a colony.
We were forced to consider how to expand trade among ourselves in this great domain. The need for East-West trade contributed to Confederation in 1867. Sir John A. Macdonald encouraged East-West trade when he built the railroad, and Prime Minister Laurier continued that trade policy.
That cycle has come to an end. We have filled the market for goods and services for 25 million Canadians. In 1988 we need a new trade arrangement and new opportunities. We have to look again to the South and create more North-South trade than we had before.
The Atlantic area always had much trade with the South, particularly the New England states. The most prosperous time in our history was when Atlantic Canada had free access to the New England area. Today, 75,000 Canadians in Atlantic Canada depend on trade for their jobs.
July 4, 1988

We need a trade agreement now because we have been facing rising protectionism in the United States. Trading blocs have been building up in the world. The European Economic Community is a major trading bloc, which gives preferential treatment to its partners. Australia and New Zealand represent another trading bloc in that area that looks after its own interests.
Who will look after our interests in this changing world where trade blocs are forming and partners are establishing preferential treatment for one another?
Prince Edward Island needs access to the United States market, where 20 per cent or more of our potatoes are sold each year. We must sell our lobsters, and 60 per cent to 70 per cent of them go to the U.S. market every year. We do not need more restrictions on those products.
One of the most successful companies in my riding is a firm called USENS Fisheries in Surrey, Prince Edward Island. That company is owned by Americans, but it provides jobs to Prince Edward Islanders for most of the year.
Its head office for the area is located in my riding. That company provides jobs and pays good money because it has access to 52 states and 250 million Americans for fish processed in Canada. That benefits workers in my riding. I am not afraid of that kind of relationship, if that is what free trade means. Free trade means a better opportunity for my children and their children.
Trading countries succeed in this world. One only need look at Japan, one of the strongest trading economies in the world. The Japanese have the lowest infant mortality rate and the longest life span. They have the lowest unemployment rates. There are many advantages to a strong economy.

Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to make a few remarks on Bill C-130. The Hon. Member who just spoke said that he was not sure what his grandparents would think about this deal. I am not sure what my grandparents would think about it.
However, what concerns me is what my grandchildren will think about it. What will our grandchildren and greatgrandchildren think about this legislation when they look back at it some years from now and ask what happened to Canada and the possibility of creating an independent, sovereign nation that was in control of its own destiny? They will ask why they are a satrapy of the United States rather than an independent and proud country.
I welcome the opportunity to speak on this Bill, particularly since the Government has introduced time allocation. There are Members who will want to make important comments on this Bill but will be unable to do so because the Government has closed off debate.
The fundamental importance of this Bill has been stressed on all sides of the House. It has been stressed by President Reagan who calls it a new economic constitution. It has been stressed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney). It has been stressed by Simon Reisman who talked about it as the greatest thing since sliced bread.
What we are dealing with here is an understanding of Canada, our vision of Canada. The vision of Canada that this Bill presents is basically that Canada is America's attic.
The United States often looks to Central America and the Caribbean as its backyard. Canada is the attic to which the Americans come to rummage around for resources, for our

July 4, 1988
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
water and our energy. They can bring down into the United States whatever they want.
The vision we in our Party have of Canada is of a nation that has a unique social and cultural contribution to make to our world. The trade agreement that the Tories are so intent upon rushing through the House would surrender this. It would surrender the possibility of this for the future. The historian Arthur Lower has pointed out that "growth into nationhood in our sphere of culture" is more difficult than the achievement of political sovereignty. That is particularly true for Canada where we live right next door to the United States with its very powerful mass market for its culture.
We share a common language with the United States. We share many of the same values. Americans have a strong popular mass culture in the areas of news, television, movies and novels. All of us from whatever Party share in a great deal of that culture.
We recognize that if we are to have an independent culture, then we have to take special measures. It is for this reason that we have seen that there has always been a much greater role for the Canadian Government to play in helping to create our Canadian culture.
The agreement states that Canada is going to be able to take those measures that it has been able to take. It can take measures to assist culture, which is okay by the agreement. However, in the very next phrase in the agreement it is stated that the United States can retaliate against Canada for taking those measures.
A culture reflects a nation. The mass culture of the United States is driven by its bottom line, by the fact that there is cash involved. Thus the Americans want to have some kind of cash compensation if Canada takes measures to protect Canadian culture. They see this as being basically a commercial transaction, and that they should be entitled to take some kind of commercial action against Canada, some type of bottom line recompense.
One of the oldest works in Canadian literature published in 1836 is Thomas C. Haliburton's The Clockmaker. The main character in his book is a Yankee trader named Sam Slick. He used to come up into Nova Scotia to sell clocks to the people of Nova Scotia. Generally speaking, he had a very low opinion of Nova Scotians. He said: "We go ahead. The Nova Scotians go astarn". The reason that he felt that was that the Yankees knew how to cipher. In other words, they were able to calculate everything to the bottom line.
At one point he said: "I tell you, if we had this country, you couldn't see the harbours for the shipping." At another point he said:
The remedy-is at hand; it is already workin' its own cure. They must recede before our free and enlightened citizens, like the Indians; our folks will buy them out, and they must give place to a more intelligent and ac-five people. They must go to the lands of Labrador, or be located back of Canada; they can hold on there a few years, until the wave of civilization reaches them,
and then they must move again as the savages do. It is decreed; I hear the bugle of destiny a-soundin' of their retreat, as plain as anything.
This is 1988 and we are talking about some of the same attitudes that the Yankees had in 1836 which they still have now in 1988.
Sam Slick was the spiritual ancestor of the present Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie). He said that he could sell clocks to people who did not really need them on the basis of his knowledge of soft sawder and human nature. If he was living today he would be selling vacuum cleaners or encyclopaedias. He might even be trying to sell the free trade agreement. He might be trying to sell things to people who do not really want them.
But, like the Minister, Sam Slick sometimes told the truth. At one point, when he was asked about the attraction of the U.S., he said:
It ain't its attraction-it's nothin' but its power of suction; it is a great whirlpool-a great vortex: it drags all the straw and chips, and floating sticks, drift-wood, and trash into it. The small crafts are sucked in, and whirl round and round like a squirrel in the cage-they'll never come out.
Not all Canadians are going to be sucked in by this trade agreement. Not all Canadians want to get caught up in the American whirlpool and get dragged in as the Tory Government seems to want to do.
Canadians do not want to be Americans. We are not anti-American-we are just different. That is important to recognize. That is something that the Conservative Party used to recognize up until the time of John Diefenbaker who recognized it. We have a different role in history. We recognize that the Americans are a great power. They have the burden and the responsibility of a great power. We might not think that they always discharge that burden and responsibility in an intelligent way, but we recognize that they have it. It is a different burden and a different responsibility from what we as Canadians have.
Canada's role is different. We are a smaller power. We have a role as a mediator. We have a different type of culture, a culture different from the mass U.S. culture. Our culture depends more on the responsibility of Government, which is why the basic organizations of Canadian culture are sponsored by the Government. I refer to such organizations as the Canadian Film Board, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the Canada Council.
The trade deal threatens all this. The fact is that the longer this debate goes on, the more people understand what this trade deal is doing to Canada. The more they understand how it threatens their culture, the more they understand how in the long term it will threaten social programs. Make no mistake about it. Business people are going to want what they call a level playing field. On both sides of the parallel they will be

Madam Speaker, I too am very pleased to take part in this debate on an extremely important issue or subject that I would call a challenge to our resourcefulness as Canadian citizens. I will be brief, merely hoping that my remarks will shed more light on a situation which some people enjoy making more confusing than it really is.
Ever since Canada and the United Sates signed the trade agreement I noticed two major trends of thought among the public. First, a noisy minority made up of Liberal and NDP Members relentlessly calls for cancellation of the agreement and maintains that Canada has sold out to the United States, that we are handing our sovereignty over to them, or so they say, in short they openly claim that we are selling the country to the Americans.
Madam Speaker, their claims are only a small part of the political picture because we must not forget that the majority of Canadian provinces are already committed to endorsing the free trade agreement.
Madam Speaker, earlier today I listened to some Members of the Opposition who said that the agreement would impose strict limits not only on the country but even more so on the provinces.
Well, Madam Speaker, either I do not understand anything at all or the provincial premiers did not even realize the Canadian Government was challenging them. Indeed, at least eight of the ten provinces-and the federal Government, of course-unreservedly support the free trade deal.
So when I hear people suggesting that we need a new mandate to justify the delay in implementing the FTA, I wonder just what kind of mandate they have in mind, once again considering that not only most Canadians but practically all provincial premiers are in favour of the agreement, including and especially Quebec.
Quebec Premier Bourassa of course agrees with the Prime Minister of Canada, they want Quebecers to forge ahead, become prosperous and get their fair share of the market.
On the other hand, Madam Speaker, the fact is that from public forums we hear about the satisfaction of business quarters and their nearly unanimous endorsement of the
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
Canada-U.S. trade deal. Those most concerned with free trade are precisely business men and women who are directly involved in commercial deals with the United States, and most of them are prepared to face up to the challenge the free-trade deal represents. They are the men and women who will make or break the agreement.
Earlier, Members of the Opposition referred to bad aspects of the agreement. Still, as Government Members we are not trying to sell something unsaleable. We are fully aware of the fact that the agreement is not without fault, that it could be improved. We are fully aware of that. But we have full confidence in mankind, in Canadian men and women, in their capacity to adapt well enough to face the free trade challenge. Big businesses, particularly those involved in resource development, have made their position known. They are united in their strong belief that they will gain from free trade.
Besides, large companies have always been a factor of prosperity for small and medium businesses, if at no other level than subcontracting. If the industrial giants gain from free trade, the same will be true for small and medium businesses, that is obvious. Not surprisingly, at this moment, about two thirds of associations representing small and medium businesses have made it known they also approved the principles of free trade.
You can see, Madam Speaker, that the so-called betrayal the Opposition is talking about does not scare business people at all. While a handful of politicians blinded by partisanship are forcing upon us the desperation of their uncertainties, the industry stopped listening to them and is intensely getting ready to forge ahead. For the last few months, we have been witnessing an important move in the business world in all industrial and commercial sectors of Canada, precisely to plan the way their relations with the United States will develop.
The message delivered by the Economic Council of Canada, the Conseil du patronat, the Chamber of Commerce, the Board of Trade, at conferences, seminars, etc . . . Madam Speaker, is quite clear: Given Canada's trade history, it is more than likely that free trade will bring about an important increase in productivity and general business activity in this country. Canada's manpower is flexible, our exchange rate is attractive and furthermore we are closer geographically to the main U. S. population centers than a number of American states such as California and Texas. Certain firms are already looking at new ways of doing business with foreign counterparts. That is what I call positive thinking. Even among American Senators and Congressmen who are avowed protectionists, the principles of free trade have recently gained support. For his part, the President of the United States is even considering some form of free trade with Mexico, thus laying the groundwork for a North American economic community.
I must admit, Madam Speaker, that no trade agreement can satisfy everyone. There will always be those who will refuse to accept the need for change and to adapt to new situations. Others still will not want to sacrifice anything temporarily,

even if the development or the future of their business depends on it. I can only ask these people to keep a cool head, to put things in their proper perspective and most of all to avoid the pitfall of emotional argumentation, since that would mean closing the door to any honest and enlightened discussion. Madam Speaker, that would mean a step toward a new type of isolation, a kind of ideological separatism, possibly more dangerous for Canada than the commercial isolation from which we have been able to get away, thanks to the courage and the determination of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
We will face the challenge, since we have many of the tools required to strike new business deals in the United States. Also, with the new Department of Industry, Science and Technology, we will be better prepared and better equipped to benefit from the free trade deal.
Madam Speaker, I ask all Canadians first to review, in an unbiased way, the past behaviour and accomplishments of the Progressive Conservative Government. Then, they will see that we have really listened to each and every group of the population. We have chosen our priorities in order to create a new harmony as far as the Constitution is concerned and to give a remarkable, and above all constant, boost to our economy. That is what we have been doing for the last three years.
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister has been successful in surrounding himself with a team knowledgeable in economic matters, and I am sincerely convinced that with the free trade agreement we will be able to further excell.
Our duty is to transcend the words and the ideologies, because we have to face the reality of the more challenging world that is awaiting us in the year 2000. So, together, with our heads held high, let us fight like we have done in the past, and the victory will be ours!

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity this evening to speak on the subamendment to Bill C-130. I wish to commence by reviewing where the so-called trade proposal came from, the Mulroney-Reagan deal, because it certainly did not come from any MPs in the House.
It originated with Ronald Reagan during his campaign to win the Republican presidential nomination in 1980. Reagan proposed a "North American accord: a new system of economic co-operation between the United States, Canada, and Mexico". Seven years later we found out what Ronald Reagan thought of it. In October, 1987, he said, "The U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement is a new economic Constitution for North America. This is our new policy, not only to Canada but to the rest of the world." What did Prime Minister Mulroney have to say during the 1984 federal election? He said, "Don't talk to me about free trade. That issue was decided in 1911. Free trade is a danger to Canadian sovereignty. You will hear no more of it from me." Who is peddling this
trade agreement now? Well, none other than John Crosbie, from the same Crosbie family, as I was reminded by the pro-Canada network when they were here in Ottawa. They reminded Members of this House that this is the same Crosbie family that, in 1949, wore the black arm band in Newfoundland, saying, "No, no, Newfoundland, don't join Canada. Join the United States". This is the same Crosbie family.
This is the same guy being held up by the Conservatives as the buffoon, the one who has never read the deal, who travels around and says, "Oh, well, I sold encyclopaedias and I never read all of them". What kind of preposterous hypocrisy! If hypocrisy was a parliamentary word I would use it to describe the present Minister of trade.
This is the Prime Minister, who, whenever any travelling American businessman came up from the United States, when he was a small boy, loved to sit on his knee and, for a buck, would sing them Oh Danny Boy.

Madam Speaker, this purely economic agreement is based on existing trade; 80 per cent of Canadian exportations go to the United States. We did not invent it. exports, can have secure access to the U.S. market, with the attendant opportunities for expansion and for developing programs in this country that are available to all Canadians, programs that will improve our quality of life and improve the productivity of all sectors of our economy, with the result, Madam Speaker, that Canadians will take greater pride and feel more independent and stronger in their Canadian identity within a market of 250 million. That is what our free trade agreement means.
Madam Speaker, when we consider that our trade with the United States provides one job out of three in this country, and when we consider that both Opposition parties would put these jobs at risk, one example being the Liberal Leader who said he would tear up the agreement... The next day he said that if they were elected, they would have to live with the agreement once it was signed. All of a sudden he was interested in international markets. We want an economic policy that looks to the future, not a regressive policy of the kind favoured by the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party, but an economic policy that reflects the will of Canadians to expand and to become independent traders in an international market.
Madam Speaker, when I hear the Opposition Members, when I hear the New Democratic Party Members tell us their stories claiming that most Canadians and Quebecers are against the agreement, they have not seen the latest polls: in Quebec, 40 per cent are in favour of free trade. Forty per cent, Madam Speaker, is a majority. And they are trying to tell us that we do not respect democracy. But what does that mean in the case of Quebec? Madam Speaker, the Government of Quebec and its Premier are in favour of the agreement; the Official Opposition is in favour of the agreement; the Conseil du patronat is in favour of the agreement; the Cooperative federee du Quebec is in favour of the agreement; Agropur and Agrinove are in favour of the agreement. I will point out to the Liberal Members who do not know Quebec that the Cooperative federee represents all farmers in Quebec and Agrinove and Agropur represent all Quebec dairy farmers.
Madam Speaker, to put in their place the Liberal Members who have not read the agreement, I will mention that Article 710 of the free trade agreement says that we keep our rights

Madam Speaker, we have given to the farmers what they wanted, we have protected them, and that is why 66 per cent or a third of their products not subjected to a quota system, for example beef or pork products, are exported to the United States. We have opened up to our producers a flourishing market, where they are more and more successful, Madam Speaker, because they have access to that market. That is nothing new, Madam Speaker, but a fact both Opposition Parties have absolutely refused to understand!
Madam Speaker, unlike members of both Parties in front of me, I view life more positively. All they know is to be negative and reactionary. Because they think that we are not able to compete with the Americans, they call Canadians a bunch of nobodies, of small-timers, and incompetent business people. Well, Madam Speaker, I am proud when I see a firm in the Champlain riding which exports to the United States, because it means my constituents can have jobs, they can buy a house, have a family, and continue to develop. That is what the future will be like for Canada and for Quebec, an optimist future centered on foreign markets and prosperity. That is what we have been aiming for with the free trade agreement.
Madam Speaker, we hear the two Opposition parties saying that Canada is being sold out to the Americans because they are ten times bigger than we are. But let's look at what is happening in other countries. Let's take, for example, Australia and New Zealand. Australia, which is seven times bigger than New Zealand, much the same, relatively speaking, as the United States compared to Canada, and New Zealand, which has increased its exports, think that the Agreement they have reached is good for both countries as a whole. The same thing applies to Sweden, which has signed a free trade agreement with other Scandinavian countries, Sweden which the New Democrats like to quote as an example of a country which has developed its social programs. They were the first to sign and to understand that an assured access to foreign markets would allow them to establish adequate social programs for their citizens and to ensure their economic development in their own environment; the European Economic Community also came to the same conclusion, Madam Speaker, and their trade has increased by 340 percent while Canada has stagnated at some 150 percent.
Such is the avenue, Madam Speaker, this Government decided to follow when the Prime Minister agreed with President Reagan to create an economic unit that would be strong for all Canadians, strong for North America, and thriving as far as economic development is concerned in the area of research, productivity and efficiency. This is how we want to open the debate, not on a negative note by telling stories about the past because it would be shameful to tell

The third category I want to discuss is the politics of the deal.
Let us examine why tariffs were originally implemented. Their purpose was to protect certain Canadian industries, which were largely in the manufacturing sector. Management would be one of the main beneficiaries of a business that was protected by these tariffs. They had a margin of error built directly into their prices with that tariff protection. Another margin of error could be applied to technological advances because they were looking at reduced investments. Those businesses did not have to be on the leading edge of competition.
However, they were not the only beneficiaries. The unions also benefited from tariff protection. They experienced job security along with reduced pressure on their need to be productive.
Of course, there were those who had to pay the price for that tariff protection. Several groups fall into that category. The first group would be the consumers who had to pay higher prices for their goods. They ended up with a limited or more restricted supply. As a result, those consumers began to pay the price of any tariff protection that existed within our economy.
There is another group that I think suffered just as much. It is a group which I think specifically relates to western Canada, that group of people who are involved in the development of our resources in the West. The reason they suffered is that the costs of goods and materials which they needed to develop, export, and market their products were higher to them simply because of the tariff protections which existed.
If one is in the oil and gas business, that means that pipe costs more because of tariff protection. Work clothes cost more because of tariff protection. The same is true with respect to tools which cost more.
All of this came to a violent head when the previous Liberal administration brought forward the National Energy Program. When that was done it became apparent to western Canadians that we were not able to buy the goods that we needed at world price. We had to pay the world price plus a tariff. We may have paid anywhere from 115 per cent to 130 per cent more for particular goods or services that we bought which were protected by tariffs. Yet, when it came to our own commodities, the commodities that we wished to sell-and under the National Energy Program that particular commodity was our oil and gas-we were told that we could not sell them at the world price. We had to go below the world price, down to 85 per cent of world price. What we had then was an obvious imbalance. Those who were protected by tariffs were receiving a premium price for their commodities. Those of us who were not protected by tariffs actually paid a penalty. In the case of the National Energy Program that penalty was 15 per cent.
It was no wonder that western Canadians were so angry about the National Energy Program. It is no wonder that their attention was focused immediately on the whole business of tariff protection. It is no wonder that today western Canadians in such a large majority support the free trade agreement.
I wish to consider why westerners support this deal. The first reason is that consumers of manufactured goods for the most part live in the West. They see prices being reduced as a result of the free trade agreement. They see more variety of goods and services being made available to them. As consumers they are in favour of the agreement.

Second, as producers of resources, whether that be in the area of oil and gas, forestry, or agriculture, they see full access to the American market. They see an opportunity to sell their goods at world price.
Third, they see the costs of their materials being reduced as a result of the reduction in those tariffs and as a result of increased competition in particular areas of supply.
The fourth reason that western Canadians support the deal is that we in the West are putting a great deal of energy into diversifying our economy. That is why the Government put into place the Western Diversification Program and why it has established the Western Diversification Office. That was done because we want to build a manufacturing and processing industry in western Canada. In order to accomplish that we need materials at lower prices, those materials that we need in order to finish or process our products.
Something else which is important in terms of the diversification of our economy is that we need access to the California market. That market consists of 25 million people who live in the State of California. That figure is roughly equivalent to the whole population of the entire country of Canada. The reality is that the California market is closer to the City of Edmonton than is Toronto or Montreal. Thus we have a larger market available to us through the free trade agreement. It is much closer to us than is the existing market in Canada. That is why we see so much opportunity and potential for diversifying our economy.
I now wish to talk about the politics of the deal. What we are really being offered is two choices. The Government is offering a positive position on free trade, what I call a balanced deal. We have negotiated a fair deal, a deal which says to the West: "Here is your chance to develop, to diversify, and to revitalize your economy. Here is a chance for those who are in the tariff protected industries to experience a phase out of those tariffs". In other words they are not hit right now, today; there is a phase down time. They have a 10-year period in some cases to make the transition from a tariff protected environment to an environment that is not protected.

speechtext:
Since opposition Members wish me to debate the subamendment, I will tell them that I will never support the subamendment. If opposition Members wish me to debate the amendment, I will tell them that I will never support the amendment, but I will support free trade, Bill C-130, because it is the only saviour of Canada.
Let me tell all Hon. Members about the great riding of Mississauga North. This little booklet contains 7,000 businesses in Mississauga just waiting to ship their goods across into the United States. We cannot wait to increase the size of the terminal at Lester B. Pearson Airport because we want to get our goods across into the United States.
The Mississauga Board of Trade conducted a survey. It was a simple survey sent out to 2,700 corporate members. The Board of Trade asked: "Are you in favour of free trade? Will your company benefit?" Fifty-eight per cent said yes, 15 per cent said no, and the rest were not sure. Perhaps some of the workers have been brainwashed by the unions and may not be supporting free trade. The entrepreneurs and the businesses are because they want to sell their goods in another country. They will, and they will create jobs.
Since the war we have become more and more dependent on trade with the United States. In 1945, 30 per cent of our exports were shipped to the United States. Today it is almost 80 per cent.
In the United Kingdom our exports have fallen from 5 per cent to 2.4 per cent. Our exports to Japan have fallen from 6.1 per cent to 5.4 per cent.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Blame it on the Tories.

We need trade with the United States and we want to secure our markets with the United States. The only way to do so is a
comprehensive free trade agreement with a good dispute settlement mechanism so that we can sell-

As the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) has stated, we do not need to know every tittle that is in there. All we need to know is that businesses in Mississauga will benefit.
Members of the NDP sit over there and laugh. There is not one among them who has ever created a job. Are they going to stand up and speak? No, they are not, because they have not a word to say. The Liberals are also sitting there. They are great while they are sitting down.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT

For the first time Canada's legitimate concerns over cultural policy, social programs, and regional development have been recognized, putting to rest the unfounded claims that freer trade leads inevitably to assimilation.
I have some other surveys here, Madam Speaker. In Alberta, 53 per cent are in favour of free trade and 32 against; 44 per cent in British Columbia are in favour of the free trade agreement.
If they want to call an election, I will fight it on free trade any time at all.

It states: "A new survey reveals the small business sector in Ontario and throughout Canada has become more positive about free trade with the United States since the signing of the agreement in January. Federation President, John Bulloch, said opposition to free trade within the small business sector of Ontario has dropped by half since CFIB conducted a similar survey among its membership in 1986". It has dropped from 15.9 per cent to 7.8 per cent.
We hear a lot from the Opposition about whether Canadians can compete. Does Canadian industry have the plants, equipment, skilled labour force, and managerial skills to take on American competition? I say that we have. Free trade to the world's largest and richest market will allow Canadian industry to specialize in producing those things we do best. The result will be more investment, more exports, and more jobs. In 1984 we promised jobs, jobs, jobs. We could have sat here and done nothing like the Liberals did from 1980 to 1984. We
July 4, 1988

promised change, not only change for the sake of change but, change for the better. We are not afraid to go out and bring forward an agreement like this one.
Much has been said about the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) changing his mind. Any politician who has not changed his mind at some time does not have a mind to change. The Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Ms. Dewar) is the former Mayor of Ottawa. I am quite sure in her term as Mayor of Ottawa she changed her mind numerous times.

We hear from their seats one or two Tories who say: "You can tear up the agreement with six months' notice". That is the excuse to say that we are not affecting future generations, because some future Government can actually rip up the agreement. They say that and they mean it. It is true that with six months' notice any Party can give notice, but let us look at what will happen. The way the Government is selling us out, it would be very difficult to unscramble those eggs and it knows that.
I was very interested when the former Conservatives Whip, the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), one of the valued dinosaurs of the Conservative Party, rose and said that he was for this agreement, that the New Democratic Party was against the agreement because we wanted a socialist Canada, and that this agreement would prevent it. What that Member was in fact stating was that future Canadian Governments were obviously limited in making decisions for this country. It is not a matter of socialism; it is not a matter of what social programs we want and what other Parties may not want. That Member was speaking the truth in his own way. He was recognizing that the ability of future Canadian Governments to make decisions that are important to Canada will be restricted by this agreement.
One thing that is interesting in terms of the Government and its desire to restrict this debate is, as we see from the Environ-ics poll, is that opposition to free trade is growing across the country. In Saskatchewan, Premier Grant Devine has been out there campaigning. Let us remember what he said-

They do not want to hear from the Conservatives. They get upset. They get upset when the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) quotes the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark). They get upset when one of our Members quotes the Conservative leadership. Now they are upset when I try to mention what a Conservative Premier says. The Conservative Premier from Saskatchewan went around the province, preaching the value of free trade, explaining how important it was to the West and actually picking on the people of Ontario. What happened? Let us take a look. Which province is most against the Mulroney trade deal? It is the Province of Saskatchewan. I recognize that I should not have said "the Mulroney trade

deal". I should have said the Prime Minister's trade deal, and I apologize, Madam Speaker. The point is that, as the Premier went out and tried to sell the deal, the people of that province turned against the trade agreement.
Let us take a look at what is happening today in the Government's latest issue. Let us look at what the Government says, in its own glossy publication. With regard to investment it asks: "What happens with the deal? What happens to future foreign investment in this country?" The Government says, in its own publication that performance requirements such as increased exports, import substitution, sourcing requirements, and/or domestic content levels as a condition of investment will not be permitted under the agreement. This means that if some foreign-owned company comes and takes over a Canadian firm, we have absolutely no right to regulate what the firm will do. It is the right of any nation to determine what will happen with its own resources, its own companies, its own regional development. We have a right, as Canadians, to make those decisions and those requirements. The Conservatives want to sell out that right. This group of Conservatives says "That is what we want. We do not want to have any controls. We do not want the Canadian Government to be able to say that it thinks, if there is a foreign takeover, that perhaps that firm should be investing in Canada, perhaps that firm should be buying goods in Canada, perhaps that firm should be hiring and training Canadians".
The Government does not want that power, and it wants to ensure that future Governments do not have that power. What I find amazing is that these Conservatives are rejecting what every other Conservative Government in the country has ever stood for. One interesting thing is that they ask: "What about the automobile industry?" Do these Conservatives remember that when the President of Ford Canada made his speech to the annual meeting-the board of directors were all there; they spoke to all their shareholders, 94 per cent being Ford of the U.S-he said that he was all for this trade agreement, that he liked this trade agreement? He congratulated the Government on it, and then he said that he did not like provincial laws on occupational health and safety. Because there was provincial laws on occupational health and safety-

The President of Ford Canada said that he did not like these laws because they restricted the company's right. Because of that, he thought that it might be just as advantageous for the company not to build a new plant in Oakville but to do it in the States.
The situation is that they are saying: "Okay, with the new trade agreement which we love, we are in a situation where we can make a decision that if we do not like provincial laws on occupational health and safety we can actually relocate in the States." That is going to be allowed under this agreement. That is going to happen as a result of this agreement.
The Government says: "We are not affecting provincial programs. We are not affecting occupational health and safety. We are not affecting the various social programs that have been put in place in the various provinces." However it is allowing Ford, GM, Chrysler, General Electric, and all such other firms to say: "Well, we don't like the social programs you have in Canada. We don't want to pay for those social programs that you have in Canada, so we are going to take our corporations, we are going to take our plants, and we are going to develop them in the southern states".
We have some controls in this country, we have the right to make decisions in this country, and they are selling out that right and they know it.
July 4 will be a Conservative holiday, and I will tell you, Madam Speaker, that my sons, my grandsons, and my granddaughters will remember the Conservatives as the traitors that they are.

this evening on this very important trade agreement between our two sovereign nations.
I feel a bit like Alice in Wonderland. Things are getting curiouser and curiouser as this debate goes on. Opposition Members demand time to debate. They say five days are not enough, but they are having trouble putting up speakers. We have just heard the Hon. Member for Churchill (Mr. Murphy) talk about the horrible Americans, as the New Democrats tend to classify them. Let us remember that it was an NDP Government in Manitoba-and the NDP Member for Churchill will be well aware of this-that sold its hydro power to the Americans.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: What?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Why did the NDP Government do that, Madam Speaker? It was to create jobs in Manitoba. That is what happens in western Canada in particular where we fund our lifestyle on the resources that we export to other nations. The NDP Government in Manitoba has done that and other Governments across this nation have done that in order to create employment. This agreement will secure that kind of an arrangement with the Americans who are one of our biggest trading partners.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT IMPLEMENTATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We are selling now without free trade.

Then we had the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) a little earlier this evening talking like Rambo Jim about American tanks at the border coming to take our water, our trees, and our fish. The Hon. Member knows full well that that is not accurate. I wonder how dumb he thinks the average Canadian voter is to accept that kind of drivel.
Our own Government in British Columbia has released a report on the free trade agreement. I know the Hon. Member from Skeena and other NDP Members are big fans of the B.C. Government. Let us listen to what is in this report. The B.C. Government predicts, through its own research, a 2.5 per cent increase in provincial Gross Domestic Product by 1999 in British Columbia and 27,600 net new jobs in B.C. through the free trade deal. The question was asked about where B.C.'s exports were destined for. Through this document it shows that 46 per cent of British Columbia's exports go to the United States, 26 per cent to Japan, and 28 per cent elsewhere. "What will free trade's impact be on B.C.'s employment? No effect: 83 per cent; positive effect; 15 per cent; negative effective"- about which our socialist friends and Liberal friends seem to be so wrapped up-"2 per cent; barely minimum".
Let us look at Vancouver Island, my particular part of the world. What will the free trade's impact be on B.C. regions, Victoria and Vancouver Island which have a labour force of
201,000	workers? There will positive effect of 14 per cent on that labour force. I wish I came from my hon. friend's riding of Skeena. Up in Prince Rupert and area-I have 14 per cent on Vancouver Island-according to this document the positive
Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement
effect in Skeena will be 28 per cent through the free trade deal. The Hon. Member stands in this Chamber and debunks one of the greatest agreements between sovereign nations. He should listen to his fellow socialists in New Zealand and Australia who have their own free trade agreement. It is working so well that they are speeding things up. They want the mechanism brought forward earlier than the 1990s.
Let us look at what has happened between Ireland and the United Kingdom. In 1963 before they signed their free trade agreement, 70 per cent of Ireland's trade was with Great Britain and 30 per cent with the rest of the world. What has happened 25 years later? That is a good example, a small country and a big country. We are all afraid of the great Americans. Twenty-five years later the situation is the reverse. Seventy per cent of Ireland's exports are to the world, the rest to Great Britain. Ireland became better at what it did. It had a larger market-place in which to trade and could export products much better. That is what will happen to Canada with this deal. Then we have our friends in the Liberal Party.

The New Democrats say that they are going to tear it down. The Liberals want more debate and want the legislative committee on Bill C-130 to travel across the country. Of course they do not really want too much input because they will tear it up anyway. Canadians will never support a potential Government that would tear up any kind of sovereign agreement. The Liberals say that they do not want a bilateral agreement with the U.S. What they want is world trade. That has been their argument for the last little while-not the U.S. but the world.
What happened when we had a world leader in this Chamber? The Prime Minister of Great Britain, Margaret Thatcher, came here. What was the Liberal reaction? Did they want to discuss trade with Margaret Thatcher? Of course not. They wanted to shout her down. They did not want to hear what she had to say about the benefits of world trade.
We have heard many quotes in this Chamber over the last few days. What have people in the B.C. forest industry said? Peter Bentley, Chairman of the Canfor Corp., has refuted claims that Canada would be better off as things are than with free trade. He said:
That assumption is a myth, and the forest industry is living proof that
protectionism in the U.S. is alive and well.
He went on to say:
Bear in mind that as Canadians tariffs have declined, our exports to the U.S.
have increased. Opponents of the agreement argue that free trade will cause
Canada to lose jobs and trade to the U.S., yet history proves just the opposite.
When tariffs come down, trade will go up.
That is all around the world, including Canada. The fishermen in British Columbia whom I know are listening to me tonight if they are not out on their boats catching fish, it is

the season. Let us see what the American fishermen are saying and here is a good indication of what free trade means. This is from an American magazine, the February issue of National Fisherman:
American east and west coast fishermen, processors, and their representatives have voiced virtually unanimous opposition to the proposed free trade agreement.
These are the Americans. Here is another quote:
-fishing industry leaders say the U.S. industry has more to lose than gain if the trade pact is ratified. They charge that the accord is unbalanced in favour of Canadian fishing interests.
As U.S. seafood industry representatives view it, the elimination of tariffs would be of substantially greater benefit to their Canadian counterparts since they would gain tariff-free access to one of the world's major seafood markets.
There you have it, Madam Speaker, from the forest industry to the fishing industry, to almost every other industry in this nation, the benefits from free trade are quite obvious. I wish I had more time. I have much more evidence and more brilliant eloquence to go through about the free trade deal. Let me summarize my comments this way as we wrap up the evening.
Many western Canadians to whom I have spoken are excited about the possibility which the free trade agreement presents. We know that Canada-U.S. trade has increased by 40 per cent over the past eight years. We do not feel any less Canadian because of that. We know that 85 per cent of our cross-border trade with the U.S. is now tariff-free and that including the remaining 15 per cent is quite logical. We know what western Canadians can do given half a chance.
Our Government is prepared to provide that opportunity in this nation through the free trade agreement with the United States of America.
